articles.title: Influencer tem surpresa em passeio com sucuri devorando pássaro em rio | G1
articles.standfirst: Roger Regis filmava uma caminhada quando encontrou as serpentes. A segunda apareceu justamente onde ele esperava encontrar outra cobra.
articles.summary: Sucuri em MS: o influencer Roger Regis registrou o encontro com duas serpentes em Ribas do Rio Pardo, incluindo o flagrante de uma delas predando um pássaro no local.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Uma caminhada no fim da tarde em uma fazenda na cidade de Ribas do Rio Pardo rendeu mais surpresas do que o influencer de aventura Roger Regis imaginava. Ele se deparou com duas sucuris, uma delas enrolada em um pássaro. Veja o vídeo acima.

A experiência foi compartilhada com os seguidores dele em um vídeo publicado nesta terça-feira (24). Após filmar filmava a primeira serpente, Roger lembrou que já havia encontrado outra sucuri em uma poça d'água mais adiante. Curioso, resolveu voltar ao local e testar a sorte.

“Vamos ver, já pensou a gente encontra duas, cara, vai ser muita sorte.”

Sucuri flagrou sucuri devorando pássaro em rio de MS. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Reprodução

Com a câmera ligada, o guia seguiu até o local e, para a própria surpresa, encontrou exatamente o que procurava. Dessa vez, porém, a sucuri estava enrolada em um pássaro.

“Uma vez eu encontrei outra cobra aqui, ó, uma sucuri aqui. Agora eu conversando com vocês, ainda bem que filmei, cara.”

Depois dos dois encontros inesperados, ainda teve tempo de apreciar o pôr do sol.

“Foi um achado hoje, finalzinho de tarde meu aqui rendeu.”

Cobras encontradas no mesmo passeio — Foto: Roger Rogis

Apesar da fama criada por histórias e filmes, a sucuri costuma evitar o contato com seres humanos. Os ataques são associados principalmente a situação em que o animal se sente ameaçado.

A sucuri-verde, uma das espécies mais comuns em Mato Grosso do Sul, é a maior entre as espécies e a que possui mais dados científicos disponíveis. Recebe o nome pela coloração verde-oliva, que pode variar do claro ao marrom escuro.

🔎Apesar de não ser a serpente mais longa (esse título pertence a píton-reticulada), a sucuri-verde é a mais pesada do mundo, podendo atingir 8 metros de comprimento e pesar até 250 kg. Seu corpo musculoso e robusto a torna extremamente forte, sendo capaz de capturar e dominar presas de grande porte, como capivaras e jacarés.

articles.title: Rodovia do Açúcar: buraco causa prejuízo e riscos a motoristas  | G1
articles.standfirst: Pelo menos 19 veículos tiveram pneus e rodas danificados no km 158 na noite desta quarta-feira (25). Motoristas denunciam risco de batida ao tentar parar no acostamento em meio ao trânsito pesado.
articles.summary: Na Rodovia do Açúcar, em Piracicaba, um buraco no km 158 danificou 19 veículos em uma única noite, gerando pneus rasgados e alto risco de acidentes na pista.
articles.body:
Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Motoristas denunciam prejuízos, com pneus furados em sequência, e riscos de acidentes provocados por um buraco na Rodovia do Açúcar (SP-308) no trecho urbano de Piracicaba (SP).

Ao menos, 19 ocorrências de carros afetados pela situação da pista foram registradas na noite desta quarta-feira (25), segundo apuração da EPTV , afiliada da Globo para região.

Uma das motoristas afetadas gravou imagens de veículos parados no acostomento após terem os pneus e rodas danificados pelas irregularidades na rodovia. Assista, acima.

Buraco em trecho da Rodovia do Açúcar, em Piracicaba (SP) — Foto: Edijan Del Santo/EPTV

O trecho com buracos na Rodovia do Açúcar fica na altura do Km 158. Além dos estragos nos veículos, os motoristas também apontaram os perigos sofridos ao terem que parar o carro bruscamente em meio ao fluxo de veículos, muitos de grande porte, na rodovia.

O veículo da auxiliar contábil, Eduarda de Souza, teve um pneu rasgado após passar por um dos buracos na pista.

"Eu ainda quase bati o carro, tinha um caminhão do lado. Conforme a batida, o pneu puxou o carro. Fiquei segurando e depois que o caminhão passou, só aí consegui encostar no acostamento. Um risco. Estou tremendo até agora de medo", contou em entrevista à EPTV.

Motoristas têm pneus de carros rasgados após passarem por buraco na Rodovia do Açúcar em Piracicaba — Foto: Edijan Del Santo/EPTV

O diretor de marketing, Jefferson Mitsumoto, seguia pela Rodovia do Açúcar no mesmo momento quando passou pelo buraco. Ele descreveu o momento e contou que cerca de outros cinco carros tiveram o mesmo problema.

"Estávamos indo pra São Paulo. Passamos do lado esquerdo. Então, por sorte foi um pneu só. Mas, tem gente que perdeu os dois. Só deu tempo de parar. Já pararam uns cinco ou seis carros. Prejuízo total. Rasgou mesmo", relatou.

O aulixiar de mecânico Osvaldo Pedro Nascimento teve prejuízo com dois pneus. Ele parou para trocar o pneu. A roda também ficou danificada. "Passei pelo mesmo buraco que todo mundo", comentou.

O fluxo intenso de veículos nas duas vias agrava o risco de colisões, já que caminhões e carros invadem faixas contrárias de forma brusca para desviar das crateras.

"Perigoso estourar um pneu. Pode ser um acidente grave ainda. É um absurdo, né? Então os pedágios daqui são caros", afirma o empresário Nelson Conde, que frequenta a Rodovia do Açúcar.

Buracos na Rodovia do Açúcar causam prejuízos a motoristas — Foto: Edijan Del Santo/Reprodução EPTV

"Está muito arriscado. Eu quase bati o carro já. Ou você joga em cima de outro carro, em cima de uma moto. Está complicado", relata o trocador de moldes Leonardo Corrêa.

"Qualquer deslize a pessoa vai. Isso daí já vem contínuo, as obras que fizeram são 'meia-boca' e o buraco ainda continua aí, está só aumentando", diz o vigilante Abraham de Sousa sobre a SP-304.

Lama em passagem de pedestres em trecho da Rodovia do Açúcar, em Piracicaba — Foto: Edijan Del Santo/EPTV

Questionada sobre a Rodovia do Açúcar, a concessionária Rodovias do Tietê informou que as equipes responsáveis pela manutenção já identificaram os problemas no trecho e que a recuperação do local entrou na programação.

Sobre a sequência de pneus furados na noite desta quinta-feira (25), a empresa não retornou aos questionamentos da EPTV até a publicação desta reportagem.

A empresa justificou que o cronograma de trabalho sofreu diversas alterações por causa das chuvas das últimas semanas.

articles.title: Rio Capivari transborda após atingir 2,52 metros; veja interdições | G1
articles.standfirst: Após chuvas de mais de 80 milímetros, manancial começou a baixar nesta segunda-feira (26), mas retomou patamar acima dos 3 metros nesta terça-feira (27).
articles.summary: Rio Capivari transborda após chuvas intensas e atinge 2,52 metros; Defesa Civil monitora pontos de alagamento e orienta moradores em áreas de risco no município.
articles.body:
Água tomou Rua Padre Haroldo, no Jardim Juventus, após enchente do Rio Capivari — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV/Arquivo

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O nível do Rio Capivari atingiu 2,52 metros após as chuvas que atingiram a região e transbordou na manhã desta quinta-feira (26).

Cerca de cinco famílias precisaram deixar casas e foram para abrigos da prefeitura. A cota de extravasamento do manancial é de 2,35 metros, segundo informações da Defesa Civil de Capivari (SP).

Cidade tem dez pontos de alagamentos, segundo balanço atualizado às 10h30 desta quinta-feira.

A cidade entrou em estado de alerta e as equipes estão mobilizadas, monitorando o nível do rio e adotando medidas preventivas, segundo a prefeitura.

Rio Capivari começa a baixar depois de atingir três metros e transbordar em Capivari — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

"Nos últimos dias, foram registrados mais de 230 milímetros de chuva na região da bacia do Rio Capivari. Além disso, uma forte chuva localizada atingiu o município na noite desta quarta-feira (25), contribuindo para a elevação do nível do rio", detalhou a Defesa Civil.

A Prefeitura de Capivari divulgou os dez pontos de alagamentos e interdições às 10h30 desta quinta-feira:

Rua João Vaz com trecho da rua Antônio Pires (Centro)

Rua João Nicolucci (Santa Rita de Cássia – Trevo)

Rua Benedito Amaral (Santa Rita de Cássia – Trevo)

Rua Carlos Pinto Antunes (Santa Rita de Cássia – Trevo)

Rua Bruno Rocco (Santa Rita de Cássia – Trevo)

Abertura das comportas da Barragem Leopoldina

Devido às chuvas intensas nas cabeceiras do Rio Capivari, a Defesa Civil informou que solicitou à empresa Raízen a abertura total das comportas da Barragem Leopoldina, como medida preventiva para facilitar o escoamento da água e minimizar os impactos no município.

A Defesa Civil orienta os moradores, principalmente aqueles que residem em áreas de risco, a permanecerem atentos ao nível do rio e às informações divulgadas pelos canais oficiais da Prefeitura.

A recomendação é que a população não atravesse ruas alagadas, seja a pé ou com veículos, e siga as orientações das equipes que atuam nos bairros.

Capivari tem dez pontos de alagamentos e interdições após rio transbordar — Foto: Defesa Civil de Capivari/ Reprodução

Em caso de emergência, a população pode acionar a Defesa Civil pelos números 199 e (19) 3492-3186.

A Guarda Civil atende pelo telefone 153 e pelo WhatsApp (19) 3491-1311, enquanto o Corpo de Bombeiros pode ser acionado pelo 193. Os serviços de emergência funcionam 24 horas por dia, todos os dias da semana.

Antes dos alagamentos desta quinta-feira, a cidade tinha enfrentado transtornos com enchentes provocadas pela cheia do Rio Capivari em outubro deste ano. Relembre no vídeo, abaixo.

articles.title: Carmim lança no Brasil dois vinhos de alta gama do terroir de Monsaraz | G1
articles.standfirst: Rótulos portugueses são trazidos e distribuídos em todo o país pela Porto a Porto.
articles.summary: Rótulos portugueses são trazidos e distribuídos em todo o país pela Porto a Porto.
articles.body:
A partir de uvas selecionadas nativas de Portugal e outras francesas, de cultivo mais recentes no Alentejo, nascem dois vinhos de alta gama assinados pela renomada vinícola Carmim e que acabam de chegar ao Brasil. São rótulos de longo amadurecimento em barrica e muito gastronômicos que vão fazer bonito nas mesas de fim de ano.

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Os rótulos da linha Monsaraz Grande Reserva DOC Alentejo expressam o melhor do terroir alentejano, que é a maior região produtora de Portugal, e se destacam pela complexidade e profundidade de aroma e sabor. Os rótulos são trazidos e distribuídos em todo o Brasil pelas importadoras Porto a Porto e Casa Flora.

Presente no mercado brasileiro há décadas, a Carmim é reconhecida pela qualidade e o excelente custo-benefício de seus vinhos. As duas novidades chegam para complementar a linha Monsaraz, que já conta com cinco vinhos no Brasil.

A linha explora o prestigiado terroir de Monsaraz, vilarejo medieval localizado na Denominação de Origem Controlada do Alentejo onde são produzidos premiados vinhos a partir de uvas tradicionais portuguesas.

Os dois lançamentos são um tinto e um branco que possuem intensidade e estrutura para acompanhar diferentes tipos de comidas.

A Monsaraz Grande Reserva DOC Alentejo Branco se destaca pelos aromas de fruta branca madura, frutos secos e notas florais. Em boca, é estruturado e intenso num conjunto fresco, complexo, com final longo e persistente.

O Branco é perfeito com bacalhau e peixes grelhados. — Foto: Divulgação/Porto a Porto.

Fermentou em barricas de carvalho francês e passou por bâtonnage, um processo em que as leveduras usadas na fermentação são remexidas periodicamente para agregarem complexidade aromática e de sabor e uma textura cremosa ao vinho. Posteriormente, estagiou nas mesmas barricas durante 18 meses.

É um vinho perfeito para acompanhar peixes assados, como bacalhau, e queijos de meia cura. As uvas usadas nesse blend são as portuguesas Antão Vaz e Viosinho.

Já o Monsaraz Grande Reserva DOC Alentejo Tinto apresenta aroma de frutos pretos maduros, como amoras e ameixas, envolto em notas de especiarias. Em boca, é amplo, fresco e profundo com boa estrutura e grande complexidade aromática. Termina com final agradável e persistente.

O Tinto vai muito bem com carnes assadas. — Foto: Divulgação/Porto a Porto.

Amadureceu em barricas novas de carvalho francês durante 16 meses e, após engarrafamento, estagiou em cave durante mínimo de 12 meses. Acompanha lindamente carnes ensopadas, cordeiro, porco assado, churrasco, linguiças e queijos curados.

É um corte de uvas portuguesas Alicante Bouschet (40%) e Touriga Nacional (20%) com as francesas Petit Verdot (20%) e Syrah (20%).

Criada em 1971 e localizada na vila de Reguengos de Monsaraz, a Carmim é a maior vinícola do Alentejo e uma das maiores de Portugal. Em cada vindima, vinhos brancos, rosados e tintos traduzem o corpo e a alma da região que possui um terroir perfeito para produções de alta qualidade.

Ali o solo é pobre, mas profundo e pedregoso, e o clima continental é marcado por invernos frios e verões quentes e secos. Todas essas condições são excelentes para o desenvolvimento da videira e o amadurecimento das uvas.

Na adega, a magia acontece sob o olhar dos enólogos Rui Veladas e Tiago Garcia, que combinam ciência e inovação com “o saber antigo”, enraizado na cultura alentejana de produzir vinho.

articles.title: Advogadas são investigadas por intermediar recados de facção em SC | G1
articles.standfirst: Foram cumpridos 1 mandado de prisão temporária e 6 de busca e apreensão. Ações ocorreram em Joinville, Jaraguá do Sul, Barra Velha, Gaspar e Chapecó.
articles.summary: Foram cumpridos 1 mandado de prisão temporária e 6 de busca e apreensão. Ações ocorreram em Joinville, Jaraguá do Sul, Barra Velha, Gaspar e Chapecó.
articles.body:
Três advogadas são alvo de operação em SC por suspeita de intermediar recados de facção criminosa — Foto: MPSC/Divulgação

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Três advogadas foram alvo de uma operação na manhã desta quinta-feira (26), em Santa Catarina , por suspeita de usar a advocacia para levar e trazer informações entre presos e membros de uma facção criminosa em liberdade. No total, foram cumpridos um mandado de prisão temporária e seis de busca e apreensão .

A ação foi realizada pelo Grupo Estadual de Enfrentamento a Facções Criminosas (GEFAC) e pelo Grupo de Atuação Especial de Combate às Organizações Criminosas (Gaeco), do Ministério Público (MP). A seccional catarinense da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil (OAB-SC) acompanha os trabalhos.

Conforme a investigação, as profissionais atuam na região Norte do estado . Os mandados judiciais foram cumpridos em Joinville , Jaraguá do Sul , Barra Velha , Gaspar e Chapecó.

Procurado pelo g1 , o MP não confirmou se umas das advogadas foi alvo do mandado de prisão. O caso corre sob sigilo, e outros detalhes não foram divulgados.

Segundo o MP, "as investigadas teriam se valido de visitas realizadas em unidades prisionais para intermediar a troca de informações entre apenados e membros da facção criminosa em liberdade".

"As diligências também indicam que, sob o pretexto de prestação de assistência jurídica, teriam ocorrido contatos destinados à transmissão de recados e orientações relacionados à atuação do grupo criminoso", diz o órgão.

Batizada de "Nuntius", a operação faz referência ao termo em latim que significa "mensageiro". Segundo o MP, o nome descreve a conduta das suspeitas, que atuavam como intermediárias na transmissão de informações.

articles.title: Governador eleito anuncia novo comandante dos Bombeiros de Roraima | G1
articles.standfirst: Arthur Henrique escolheu o coronel Jefferson Abreu para chefiar a corporação militar no estado. Indicação foi divulgada nesta quarta-feira (25) no Instagram.
articles.summary: Arthur Henrique escolheu o coronel Jefferson Abreu para chefiar a corporação militar no estado. Indicação foi divulgada nesta quarta-feira (25) no Instagram.
articles.body:
Arthur Henrique (PL) anuncia coronel Jefferson de Abreu como comandante-geral do Corpo de Bombeiros de RR. — Foto: Divulgação/Ascom Arthur Henrique

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

O governador eleito de Roraima, Arthur Henrique (PL), anunciou o coronel Jefferson Dayson Ribeiro de Abreu como futuro comandante-geral do Corpo de Bombeiros de Roraima. A indicação foi divulgada nesta quarta-feira (25), em um vídeo publicado no Instagram.

O anúncio ocorre durante a transição entre a atual gestão, do governador interino Soldado Sampaio (Republicanos), e a equipe de Arthur. Nas Eleições de 2026, o governador eleito recebeu 69,13% dos votos válidos no primeiro turno.

Ao anunciar o nome, Arthur destacou que a corporação, que também abrange a Defesa Civil, é essencial para enfrentar os reflexos da crise hídrica no estado a partir de janeiro de 2027.

"Quando eu assumir, vamos encontrar uma crise hídrica que pode trazer focos de incêndio por todo o nosso estado e doenças respiratórias para as pessoas. E nós temos que estar preparados para enfrentar", afirmou Arthur ao anunciar o coronel.

Roraima está em situação de emergência por causa da seca desde setembro. Segundo dados do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), o estado somou 2.919 focos de calor entre janeiro e 25 de novembro deste ano.

No vídeo, o coronel Abreu afirmou que o foco da gestão será o atendimento à população e o suporte à tropa.

"O que a gente tem a prometer é a valorização de cada um dos nossos militares do Corpo de Bombeiros, e muita excelência, ética e dedicação no trato com a população roraimense", disse o futuro comandante.

Jefferson Dayson Ribeiro de Abreu tem mais de 25 anos de carreira no Corpo de Bombeiros Militar de Roraima. Ao longo da trajetória na corporação, atuou tanto na área operacional quanto na gestão administrativa e orçamentária.

Ele já exerceu os cargos de comandante operacional da capital e do interior, secretário executivo da Defesa Civil Estadual, diretor de Prevenção e Serviços Técnicos e diretor de Gestão Orçamentária.

O militar também atuou na formação de oficiais, como instrutor de atendimento pré-hospitalar, e participou de ações de fiscalização e prevenção contra incêndios nos municípios do interior.

articles.title: Six killed, including children, in plane crash off Mississippi coast
articles.summary: US authorities are investigating the reason behind the crash that killed members of the Stokes and Knox families.
articles.body:
First responders have found the bodies of six members of two families, including three children, killed in a small plane crash off the coast of Mississippi, United States.

Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash on Tuesday. Relatives said they were on their way home from a fishing trip.

The passengers were members of two families returning home to Fort Myers, Florida, from New Orleans Lakefront airport, Louisiana.

The plane’s pilot, Brent Stokes, 50, was president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. Stokes’s company’s website described him as an “avid fisherman and life time boater”.

The other victims were Stokes’s 16-year-old son, Hunter; Stokes’s sister, Arlyn Knox, 43; her husband, Michael Knox, 43; and their two sons, 12-year-old Charles Holden Knox and 10-year-old Truett Knox.

Lynd said autopsies are being performed on Brent Stokes and Michael Knox, who was also a licensed pilot.

Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating on the water, according to coastguard spokesperson Juan Ros.

Divers found their bodies in the fuselage part of the plane after the Cessna 210 went down in the Gulf of Mexico between Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Horn Island, which is part of the Gulf Islands National Seashore.

The Knox and Stokes families confirmed their deaths in an emailed statement provided to The Associated Press news agency.

“They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family,” the statement said.

The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported at about 3:45pm (21:45 GMT) on Tuesday that it had lost contact with the aircraft, according to the coastguard.

Shortly before losing contact with the plane, an air traffic controller at Gulfport–Biloxi International airport advised the pilot of precipitation and adverse weather in the area.

The plane had been flying at about 9,000 feet (2,743 metres), above the bottom of the cloud layers when it began descending rapidly in a right-hand turn, according to FlightAware tracking data analysed by Steven Arroyo, a retired airline captain with 50 years of flying experience.

“It’s highly, highly irregular,” Arroyo told AP. “I think it’s safe to say this aircraft had some serious problems.”

Todd Curtis, an aviation expert and former Boeing safety engineer, said that nothing appeared out of the ordinary based on the publicly available audio recordings.

But he noted that precipitation in below-freezing temperatures can cause dangerous icing, potentially leading to inaccurate instrument readings or loss of lift. It is unclear whether the plane had a de-icing system.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Old office partitions, floor tiles and other structures from Delhi's iconic North Block are being removed to transform the former seat of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Old office partitions, floor tiles and other structures from Delhi's iconic North Block are being removed to transform the former seat of governance into Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum. A visit to the site of the upcoming inaugural gallery offers a glimpse into the massive restoration underway to return the historic building to its original grandeur.Eventually with a spread of nearly 1.8 lakh square metres, the museum project atop Raisina Hill is scheduled to be completed by March 2031 and is being pitched as the museum with the largest display area in the world.Focused on the civilisational journey, it will be based across North and South Block, which till recently housed the ministries of home and finance and PMO, MEA and defence respectively. The first gallery themed "Adornment" is expected to be ready for opening to the public late next year.The office of home minister in North block and Prime Minister in South Block will not be converted to a gallery and will be retained for visitors to see, culture secretary Vivek Aggarwal said.On Wednesday, TOI visited North Block where the first gallery will showcase around 1,000 artefacts and objects.The 4,500-year-old bronze figurine known as the 'Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-Daro', currently at National Museum, will be moved to the new facility as a key display later next year. Visitors can also expect to see the Nizam's jewels, and ancient gold and gem-studded jewellery from Taxila (Taksasila). Miniature paintings, sculptures from the collection from Indian Museum in Kolkata and Gandhara collection of sculptures will also be showcased.Aggarwal said that the gallery will showcase to the world India's aesthetics and sophistication through jewellery and design in decorations reflecting the civilisational journey.Not too long ago these corridors were lined with office spaces erected over the decades occupying one half of the corridors. Now large hall size rooms open up into majestic double corridors with high arches bearing red tile work highlighting the domical vaults constructed using ancient masonry technique called corbelling - an artistic element of the building.The courtyard at the centre of the corridor will be eventually curated into areas for exhibiting artefacts and scluptures showcasing the theme of the gallery to be located in the rooms.Aggarwal shared that the restoration work under supervision of experts is being conducted after an intensive survey to ensure the structure can be strengthened without disturbing the original architecture. The restoration is being carried out by CPWD under the guidance of a team from Bhopal based School of Plannning and Architecture and conservation team of ministry of culture.He said that the museum will have orientation centres, immersive experiences, food and beverage zones, curio shops and a lot more for visitors - with the main entry being from the Rakab Ganj gurdwara side where the metro station named after the museum is under construction and is expected to open in 2029.The rotunda is a majestic round room with dome where immersive experiences will welcome visitors after they enter from the main entry. Each of the two blocks have seven courtyards and one rotunda (round room with a dome). articles.title: Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court cancels major power contract
articles.summary: The court’s five-to-four ruling ends Luma Energy’s operations after a contentious legal battle.
articles.body:
In a tight vote, Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court has ruled in favour of ending the government’s contract with Luma Energy following a controversial legal battle with the private power company.

The five-to-four ruling made public on Wednesday envisions a one-year transition period.

Power outages have continued to dog the Caribbean island since Hurricane Maria inflicted vast damage to power infrastructure in 2017, leading to years of bitter recriminations over financial and policy autonomy in the US territory.

The San Juan government sued Luma nearly a year ago, following up on a campaign promise made by Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez to cancel the contract.

Luma has faced protests for years from Puerto Ricans, who raised concerns about the cost and quality of its services.

Gonzalez said her administration would seek a new company within the year awarded by the court. She assured that transmission and distribution operations would not revert to Puerto Rico’s Electric Power Authority, from which Luma had initially taken over in 2021.

She blamed Luma for “constant interruptions” and “unnecessary outages”, asserting they have enough funds to provide proper service, as she accused the company of driving the cost of electricity in the territory to record highs.

Meanwhile, a federal control board that oversees the island’s finances issued a statement saying its immediate concern is the continuity of power services.

“The Puerto Rican government’s decision to terminate the contract creates enormous uncertainty at a time when the people and businesses of Puerto Rico look for stability,” the board said, noting that there is no “clear plan or successor company in place”.

But Gonzalez rejected those concerns, bluntly saying, “There will be no chaos.”

With the narrow ruling came allegations that judges had been pressured to vote in favour of cancellation.

Judge Angel Colon Pérez, who voted against the cancellation, asserted that the final ruling stemmed from “an excessive eagerness to satisfy a capricious request from the leader currently in power”, in an apparent reference to the governor.

However, Judge Roberto Feliberti Cintron, who was part of the majority vote, sharply denied the allegations.

“We do not bow to external pressures, we do not yield to intimidation, nor do we allow smear campaigns to influence the exercise of our judicial function,” Cintron wrote. “Our obligation is to the Law, Justice, the People, and our conscience.”

“In light of the serious allegations that have been raised publicly regarding attempts to influence the Court, we reiterate our call for an immediate, rigorous, and transparent investigation,” it said.

The company said in a statement on Wednesday that it disagrees with the court’s decision but will respect the judicial process and is “carefully evaluating all available legal alternatives”.

articles.title: A German woman sat crying on a children's playground bench while speaking to her aunt on the phone; municipal officers fined her €25 for being there without a child, calling it a "mild and proportionate" measure
articles.summary: A 31-year-old woman in Germany was fined €25 after sitting on a bench at a children's playground while crying and speaking to her aunt on the phone.
articles.body: A 31-year-old woman in Germany was fined €25 after sitting on a bench at a children's playground while crying and speaking to her aunt on the phone. The incident took place on October 25, 2026, at Glückaufpark in Gelsenkirchen, in the country's western Ruhr region. The woman, identified as Hana, said she was dealing with personal and financial difficulties when she went for a walk and became overwhelmed by her emotions. Three municipal public-order officers approached her and asked whether she was accompanying children. When she said she was not, they issued her a penalty for being inside the playground without a child. The city administration defended the officers, describing the €25 payment as a "comparatively mild and proportionate measure".Three officers approach woman at German playgroundAccording to German broadcaster WDR, Hana had been experiencing considerable pressure because of her university studies and financial difficulties. She decided to go for a walk to clear her head and visited Glückaufpark in the Hassel district of Gelsenkirchen.During the walk, she became emotional and started crying. She then sat on a bench within the children's playground area and called her aunt to discuss her personal problems.While she was on the phone, three employees of the city's Kommunaler Ordnungsdienst (KOD), or municipal public-order service, approached her. They reportedly asked whether two boys playing nearby were her children.When Hana said they were not, the officers requested her identification and informed her that she had violated the playground regulations. She was subsequently issued a €25 warning payment.Hana said she would have preferred the officers to ask whether she was alright and explain the restriction before issuing a penalty.Why was she fined for sitting on a playground bench?The penalty was based on Section 12 of Gelsenkirchen's municipal public-order ordinance, known as the Ordnungsbehördliche Verordnung.The regulation states that children's playgrounds are intended for children up to the age of 14. Other adults are permitted to remain there only if they are the parents, guardians or supervisors of children present at the playground.This means the restriction does not apply only to adults using playground equipment. It also covers adults who sit on benches within the designated playground area without accompanying children.The regulation is intended to reserve children's recreational spaces for children and the adults responsible for supervising them. Violations can attract warning payments of up to €55 under the provisions reported at the time.What did the city administration say about the €25 penalty?The Gelsenkirchen city administration defended the municipal officers, arguing that they were enforcing an existing regulation rather than penalising Hana for crying or making a phone call.City spokesperson Martin Schulmann described the €25 warning payment as a "comparatively mild and proportionate measure".The administration said the municipal public-order service was responsible for enforcing local regulations and that violations were dealt with consistently, while taking proportionality and equal treatment into account.The city also said an internal review had found no evidence of inappropriate behaviour or an improper tone during the interaction. It maintained that the officers had acted within the applicable rules.Why did Hana object to the officers' actions?Hana said she understood the importance of rules intended to protect children but questioned the way they were enforced.Speaking to WDR, she explained that she did not know adults without accompanying children were prohibited from sitting on benches within the playground area. She felt the officers could have first asked whether she needed help before explaining the restriction.She also argued that a simple request to move to another bench would have been sufficient.Her criticism centred on the absence of compassion during an emotionally difficult moment rather than solely on the €25 payment. She said she felt that the officers had treated her without considering the circumstances in which they found her.Hana eventually paid the amount to avoid the possibility of additional administrative costs. However, she continued to question why the officers had not issued a verbal warning first.The playground sign has also become part of the controversyAnother detail in the incident concerns the information displayed at the playground.According to reports by German media outlets, the sign at the location included pictograms outlining playground restrictions and specified an age limit of 14 years. However, it reportedly did not explicitly explain that adults without accompanying children were prohibited from sitting on the benches.Hana said she was unaware of the restriction.This has added another dimension to the controversy, with questions about whether visitors can reasonably be expected to understand the full implications of a regulation when the signage does not clearly explain every restriction.The city, however, maintained that the municipal ordinance applied regardless of whether Hana knew about it.Local politicians react to the incidentThe case also prompted reactions from political representatives in Gelsenkirchen, with different parties expressing views on how playground regulations should be enforced.Wiebke Wexeler of the Green Party's city council group told WDR that regulations should not be enforced so rigidly that they unnecessarily restrict people's use of public spaces or criminalise minor behaviour. She called for greater care in exercising enforcement discretion.The Social Democratic Party (SPD) council group said a warning would have been sufficient in Hana's case, although it continued to support the general playground regulations.Meanwhile, Simon Nowack of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) defended the restriction, arguing that children's playgrounds were intended for children and that adults without accompanying children should generally not be present.Hana also acknowledged the importance of protecting children but argued that enforcement should involve greater sensitivity and discretion.Gelsenkirchen considers increasing playground penaltiesThe incident came amid a wider discussion about penalties for violating local public-order regulations.On November 17, 2026, Gelsenkirchen's city council discussed proposals to increase penalties for several violations, including unauthorised presence on children's playgrounds.According to WDR's November 20 report, the proposed changes included increasing the warning payment for unauthorised presence on children's playgrounds from €55 to €60 and for smoking on playgrounds from €35 to €60. The penalty for spitting sunflower seeds on the ground was proposed to rise from €25 to €55. The city also proposed a €60 penalty for remaining at recreational sports facilities after 10 pm.If approved, the changes would increase the financial consequences for several violations of local public-order regulations.You use AI every day. articles.title: Changing Ends season four: Alan Carr suggests show could end in the 80s
articles.summary: Changing Ends is based on Carr's childhood in the 1980s growing up in Northampton.
articles.body:
Comedian Alan Carr said the next series of his autobiographical sitcom Changing Ends may be the last.

A Christmas special of the show, which is based on Carr's childhood in 1980s Northampton, is set to air on ITV, followed by a fourth series in 2027.

His father, Graham, was manager of the town's football club, and the next instalment of the sitcom is set to cover his dad's sacking.

Carr said: "Growing up in Northampton, I never once thought anyone would be interested in my life… it's so surreal."

The show follows a young Carr, played by Oliver Savell, as he navigates secondary school during the mid to late-1980s.

He previously told the BBC the show, which he co-wrote, was a "love letter" to his hometown.

Speaking on the Once Upon A Time podcast , Carr said: "We've got the fourth series coming out and the Christmas special, which is great. My dad ends up getting fired.

"And then we'll have to sort of see where we take it, is there one more one-hour special, a sort of one-off, I don't know? It would be nice to put a few things there."

Asked about carrying on into the 1990s, he said: "I think it's an 80s show, that's the thing. I do like writing it for the 80s."

Graham Carr was sacked from Northampton Town in May 1990 after their relegation back to the Fourth Division, and then went on to manage Blackpool and Maidstone, before returning to Northamptonshire to take charge at Kettering Town in 1992.

The 50-year-old comedian said his dad "absolutely loves" the show, and the whole family were astonished by the set.

He praised the show's art department, saying the version of his bedroom was "spot on", including his birdwatching books and tickets from the now-defunct ABC cinema in Northampton.

Carr added his dad was so convinced by the recreation of their Northampton home he almost "plunged to his death" trying to climb the false staircase on the set.

articles.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
articles.summary: Female protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, a rights group says.
articles.body:
In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.

He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."

Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.

Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

articles.title: How Silicon Valley became central to Israel’s war on Palestinians
articles.summary: From surveillance systems to AI targeting, US tech giants are deeply embedded in Israel’s war machine.
articles.body:
Activists have cited the Israeli military’s reported use of Amazon’s cloud infrastructure to upload millions of images of Palestinians as further evidence of the deep entrenchment of Western, and principally US, technology in Israel’s military and economic ecosystem.

According to rights groups and analysts interviewed by Al Jazeera, the trade in the technology and expertise that Israel relies on to monitor, track and kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza involves many of the United States’s leading technology companies, including Google, Palantir, and Microsoft. And, as Al Jazeera reported earlier this year, some of that technology has also been exported to Western governments publicly critical of Israel and its actions.

In January 2024, the US tech giant Palantir agreed to a strategic partnership with Israel’s Ministry of Defence for “war-related missions”, while Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing platform was reported to have been used to store vast archives of intercepted Palestinian phone calls that sources said helped guide deadly air strikes.

Google and Amazon, meanwhile, provide the Israeli military with advanced facial recognition and artificial intelligence capacity as part of the $1.2bn Project Nimbus .

And the US chipmaker Nvidia has become so central to the Israeli economy that economists have credited its tax payments with helping to reduce the country’s fiscal deficit.

“It’s everywhere,” said Jalal Abukhater of the digital and social rights group 7amleh, describing the surveillance Palestinians live under every day. “If you’re in East Jerusalem or Hebron, you’re being photographed. When I go to the running track, my picture is taken countless times at checkpoints or by roadside cameras.

“The 3.5 million images uploaded to Amazon are nothing. Everyone is photographed all the time, and it’s all getting fed into these systems that we don’t know about and for reasons they don’t explain.”

The rightward shift in Silicon Valley over recent years has been accompanied by more overt support for Israel.

Palantir, in particular, has been unapologetic in its support for the country throughout its genocidal war on Gaza. In July 2025, UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese found “reasonable grounds” to believe the company had provided predictive policing technology and an AI platform to Israeli forces, adding that, had proper due diligence been undertaken, technology firms such as Palantir would have divested from Israel “long ago”.

In January 2024, the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre, an international nonprofit that tracks corporate conduct, logged numerous allegations that Palantir technology had been used in Israeli attacks on Gaza. Palantir has denied abetting war crimes and denied developing the Israeli military’s Lavender and Gospel AI-assisted targeting systems.

However, Open Intel, which tracks corporate involvement in the war, has said Palantir’s software is linked to the Israeli military’s integration of intercepted communications, satellite imagery and other data to help compile military targeting lists.

Project Nimbus has also emerged as a key plank of US technology’s support for Israeli operations in the West Bank and Gaza. According to Albanese’s report, Amazon and Google stepped in when Israel’s cloud and AI infrastructure became overloaded following the beginning of its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

And OpenAI’s models have also reportedly found their way into the Israeli military’s operations, with access provided through Microsoft’s Azure platform. Leaked documents published in January 2025 showed that the military began buying access to OpenAI’s GPT-4 in August 2023, with its use of the model increasing 20-fold following the start of the Gaza war.

In a statement to Al Jazeera, OpenAI said it “does not have any contracts with Israeli military or intelligence entities”.

“We do not control which entities Microsoft contracts with through Azure. At OpenAI, we have a rigorous process for assessing whether a proposed deployment of our technology to any national security entity aligns with our National Security Principles,” the company said in its statement.

Analysts have also pointed to the connections between the US’s foremost tech giants and the Israeli military, specifically, members of the military’s cyberwarfare Unit 8200. In 2025, Drop Site News reported that a database of current and former members of Israeli military intelligence showed about 1,400 working at US tech firms, some 900 of them from Unit 8200, including roughly 250 at Microsoft, and others at Nvidia, Meta, Google, Intel and Apple.

The overlap in personnel raises questions about potential conflicts of interest. That is particularly relevant in the case of Microsoft, where serious concern was reported at a senior level that some employees in Israel had not been transparent about how Unit 8200 was using its technology.

The Guardian reported earlier this year that a Microsoft inquiry looked into how some Israel-based employees “had felt conflicting loyalties” to the company and the Israeli military.

Paul Biggar, one of the founders of Tech for Palestine, said that Israeli military personnel are embedded across US tech companies.

“Often, members of Unit 8200 are hired at senior levels and, as is often the case, they will hire people with similar technology and intelligence backgrounds to create a culture tied to their original unit,” Biggar said.

“You have to remember, these guys are spies,” he continued, “So the number one thing they want to do is bring in more people from Unit 8200 to increase their influence, including, for example, acquiring Israeli companies into US Big Tech”

Beyond the $1.2bn value of the Project Nimbus contract awarded to Google and Amazon, hard figures for the extent of the trade between Israel and US tech are hard to come by.

Irrespective of the sums of money, the heft of the Israeli military and US technology have combined to create one of the most surveilled populations on the planet.

“I’ve been lucky, but when people closer to me told me of having been pulled in [by the security services], they’ve been presented with a heat map of their entire lives,” Abukhater said, “Through a mixture of telephone tracking and constant surveillance, they’re shown where they’ve been and how long they spent there.

“We don’t even know half of it. When Microsoft’s role was exposed [in 2025], they revealed 200 million hours of audio recordings on a server in the Netherlands. That’s just one. Who else knows what they have and what these companies are processing?”

A Microsoft spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “Microsoft conducted an investigation into the alleged use of our technologies for the mass surveillance of civilians by the Israeli Ministry of Defence. In June, we published a final report summarising the investigation and outlining steps we are taking to strengthen our governance and oversight.

“This included establishing a process where any employee can anonymously report concerns about practices that may violate the company’s policies regarding the development and deployment of our technology through our Microsoft Integrity Portal,” the spokesperson added.

A spokesperson for Amazon Web Services told Al Jazeera: “We respect the privacy of our customers, and we do not discuss our relationship without their consent, or have visibility into their workloads. Customers regularly visit our offices for briefings and meetings with our teams, and any suggestion that these visits are anything other than routine customer engagement is wrong and unsubstantiated.”

A spokesperson for OpenAI told Al Jazeera: “OpenAI does not have any contracts with Israeli military or intelligence entities. We do not control which entities Microsoft contracts with through Azure. At OpenAI, we have a rigorous process for assessing whether a proposed deployment of our technology to any national security entity aligns with our National Security Principles.”

Palantir, Google, Nvidia, and the Israeli military did not respond to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment.

articles.title: Gaza meningitis cases surge as collapsing infrastructure fuels health fears
articles.summary: Meningitis is raising alarm in Gaza, where overcrowding, damaged sanitation are putting children at risk.
articles.body:
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – For the third time in less than a month, five-year-old Omar Abu Fayed has been admitted to the isolation ward at Gaza City’s Rantisi Children’s Hospital after developing symptoms of meningitis.

Each time, his mother, Zakia Abu Fayed, thought he was recovering. But days after being discharged, his fever and pain returned.

“He doesn’t even spend a full week at home before we have to bring him back,” the 24-year-old Zakia told Al Jazeera.

Omar’s illness began with a high fever, severe headache and abdominal pain. He stopped eating, and his temperature rose above 40 degrees Celsius (104F). After five days of treatment at home with fever medication and antibiotics, his condition had not improved, so Zakia took him to hospital, where doctors diagnosed meningitis.

He was admitted for five days and discharged after responding to treatment. But about a week later, the fever returned, and he spent another 10 days in hospital.

The symptoms returned days after his second discharge, and doctors changed his treatment for a third time.

“I hope he responds this time,” she said.

The repeated admissions have left her worried not only about Omar but also about her two younger children, aged three and one. She said the hospital was crowded with children suffering from meningitis, including newborn babies.

Zakia, originally from Jabalia in northern Gaza, believes Omar may have contracted the infection at kindergarten, although its source has not been established. The family has been displaced because of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and is renting a house.

Zakia’s concerns come as Gaza’s Ministry of Health warns of a sharp increase in meningitis cases . On November 24, the ministry declared an epidemic alert, reporting 272 cases in October – up sharply from the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.

The ministry said 108 of October’s cases were bacterial meningitis, compared with the usual 10 to 20 a month. A further 100 bacterial cases were recorded during the first weeks of November.

It also reported 15 deaths from the disease since the beginning of 2026, including five between August and October.

Meningitis is an inflammation of the membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. It can be caused by viruses or bacteria. Bacterial meningitis is particularly dangerous because it can progress rapidly and cause death or lasting complications, including hearing loss and neurological damage.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that limited laboratory capacity is making it difficult to distinguish between viral and bacterial infections. The UN has also reported shortages of laboratory supplies and essential medicines, with about 42 percent of essential medicines at zero-stock levels in October.

These shortages are adding to the pressure on Gaza’s already weakened health system , as overcrowding and poor sanitation leave displaced families struggling to protect themselves from infection.

At Rantisi Children’s Hospital, paediatrician Sharif Matar said the current wave began about a month ago and was continuing, although daily admissions had fallen.

“At one stage, we were receiving more than 10 cases a day. Now we are talking about three to four cases daily. There has been a decline, but the wave has not ended,” Matar told Al Jazeera.

Meningitis cases occur seasonally in Gaza, he said, but this year’s increase has placed additional pressure on hospitals. Rantisi is one of the few remaining hospitals providing paediatric services in Gaza, he added, receiving children from across the territory.

Matar linked the spread of infections to overcrowding in displacement camps and tents, where families have limited access to water and facilities for personal hygiene.

“People are living in tents, with severe overcrowding and without sufficient means of maintaining personal hygiene,” he said.

Matar said Rantisi had not recorded any deaths directly attributed to meningitis during the current wave, to his knowledge. However, some children had developed serious complications, including hearing loss and hydrocephalus, which can require surgery to relieve pressure caused by fluid building up in the brain.

He acknowledged that some medicines were occasionally unavailable, but said the hospital had so far been able to obtain the treatments required for its meningitis patients through the Ministry of Health’s medical warehouses.

“We have not reached a point where we can say that a particular essential medicine is completely unavailable,” he said.

For another mother at Rantisi, the illness has struck her six-month-old twins one after the other. Aya Salem, 29, said she had spent nearly 15 days going between hospital wards as her son Yaman and daughter Yumna became ill.

Yaman first developed a high fever about two weeks ago. After initially being kept under observation and discharged, he was brought back two days later with fever, diarrhoea and a skin rash. Doctors diagnosed meningitis, and he remained in hospital for 10 days.

As he was discharged, his twin sister’s condition worsened. Yumna was admitted with a fever that reached between 39C and 39.7C (102.2F-103.5F), accompanied by severe diarrhoea and vomiting, and was also diagnosed with meningitis. She was unable to breastfeed or take formula.

Doctors treated her with intravenous fluids, medication and zinc supplements. Her fever finally subsided the night before the interview, her mother said, but she remained unwell and had lost considerable weight.

“The doctor told me that she was among the most difficult cases. I was shocked,” Aya said.

She said she had taken precautions to protect the twins, rarely leaving their accommodation for six months except for essential errands, avoiding distribution points and not allowing visitors. But she still did not know how they had become infected.

“We live among displaced people. Every day, you do not know who your neighbour is or who might come into the area. I am extremely careful, but I do not know what happened,” she said.

She described the difficulty of maintaining hygiene in the place where the family is staying, saying there was no reliable access to clean water or adequate sanitary conditions.

Her fear is compounded by the loss of her daughters, Ayloul and Amal, who were also twins and were killed, aged three, during the war in an Israeli air strike in Gaza City on December 19, 2023.

Now, as she watches Yaman and Yumna being treated in hospital, she is pleading for action to improve the conditions in which families are living.

“Enough of what is happening to our children in Gaza. Please intervene and help improve the shattered living conditions people are facing,” she said.

articles.title: War and drought threaten livelihoods of Sudan’s farmers
articles.summary: Attacks on electricity infrastructure and drought are threatening Sudan’s harvests and leaving millions without water.
articles.body:
Haider Mohamed has worked as a farmer in Sudan’s Northern State for more than 40 years, growing fava beans, wheat, and a variety of seasonal crops.

But Sudan’s water crisis – a combination of lower-than-average rainfall and war-induced devastation to infrastructure – has severely affected his harvest and his income.

It’s a situation Mohamed describes as unprecedented in his 40 years of farming.

Mohamed owns a small farm covering about four hectares (about 10 acres) in al-Saleem, near the city of Dongola. He keeps part of his harvest to feed his family, and then sells the rest at local markets to cover essential living expenses, including healthcare and his children’s education.

“Our crops were destroyed last year, and this year it is difficult to generate any income because we are still facing electricity and irrigation problems,” Mohamed told Al Jazeera, referring to drone attacks on power stations that disrupted electricity supplies, and regularly stopped him from using electricity-dependent irrigation systems. “We have accumulated a lot of debt, and we fear that we will not harvest enough to feed our children, let alone have any surplus to sell in the market.”

Mohamed’s experience is far from unique. Across Northern State and other parts of Sudan, water shortages caused by declining rainfall or disruptions to irrigation are increasingly threatening agricultural production and the livelihoods of farming communities.

“Those who rely on diesel-powered pumps [for irrigation] cannot find fuel, and when it is available, it is extremely expensive,” Mohamed explained. “We also cannot afford the cost of installing solar-powered irrigation systems. At this rate, no one will be able to continue farming in this country.”

The ongoing war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in 2023, has severely disrupted fuel supplies in the country. Attacks on Sudan’s largest oil refinery, as well as fuel depots and petrol stations, have exacerbated shortages.

In just October, attacks blamed on the RSF damaged critical infrastructure across 11 states, disrupting electricity and water services and disabling several water supply sources.

Rising global energy prices have also made imports more expensive, with the United Nations reporting that the price of diesel nearly doubled between March and August this year.

In Sudan’s rain-fed agricultural regions, drought has compounded the problems facing farmers.

Rainfall during this year’s June-to-September rainy season declined across most of Sudan’s agricultural areas, believed to be linked to the ongoing global El Nino phenomenon. In the southeastern states of Gedaref and Sennar, rainfall was approximately 30 percent and 20 percent compared with normal levels, respectively, according to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

The two states normally account for about a quarter of Sudan’s sorghum production – the country’s main staple cereal.

The impact of the water crisis extends beyond the agricultural sector, affecting millions of people struggling to access drinking water and meet their basic household needs.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) says damage to water and electricity systems and other civilian infrastructure has deprived millions of people of essential services, while disruptions to water supplies have increased the risk of cholera and other waterborne diseases.

The UN children’s agency, UNICEF, estimates that more than 27 million people in Sudan are in need of water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance.

Between January and June of this year, UNICEF and its partners provided 6.6 million people with access to safe water, with approximately two-thirds of those receiving emergency assistance, including displaced people, those who had returned home and communities affected by conflict and cholera.

In the capital Khartoum, residents are still forced to stand in long queues for water, sometimes waiting for hours. Widespread disruptions to water supply networks and the shutdown of several water stations due to damage sustained during the war have left many households without a reliable water supply.

Saleh Zaki, who lives in Khartoum State’s East Nile district, said the area has suffered from water supply problems for many years, even before the outbreak of the war.

“Before the war, we repeatedly sought help from the authorities, only to be told there was no budget to address the problem,” Zaki said. “We therefore raised funds ourselves and hired a specialist to drill two wells, providing residents with limited water supply.”

“Since the conflict damaged the water networks … we urgently need more wells, repairs to the supply networks and solar-powered systems to support our neighbourhood and nearby communities,” he added.

In August, the Sudanese government announced a series of measures designed to ease the water crisis and encourage families displaced by war to return home.

These measures include exempting solar panels imported for personal use from customs duties, taxes, and other government fees, and waiving residential water fees nationwide until the end of 2026.

However, these measures remain limited in their impact unless accompanied by broader economic policies.

“These measures should be expanded to include greater government support for the agricultural sector, incentives for farmers, and easier access to financing for solar energy systems for agricultural use,” said Mohamed Elnayer, an economist at the Sudan University of Science and Technology. “More comprehensive reforms are also needed in the housing and agricultural sectors, particularly to rehabilitate and improve water stations, expand access to reliable water supplies, and reduce the costs of essential infrastructure.”

articles.title: At least 13 dead in Indonesia gold mine flood as rescue efforts intensify
articles.summary: Rescue workers facing tough conditions, with narrow, deep and slippery excavation pits and minimal lighting.
articles.body:
At least 13 workers have died and 13 others remain missing after flooding hit an unauthorised gold mine in Indonesia’s West Java province.

Local search and rescue chief Desiana Kartika Bahari confirmed the death toll in a statement on Thursday, as rescuers battled high water, darkness and slippery, narrow terrain in search of the missing workers.

Police first received reports of trapped miners on Tuesday, about 16 hours after the flooding occurred, police said, while nearby state-owned mining company PT Antam forwarded a formal report to the Jakarta Search and Rescue Agency shortly after midnight on Wednesday, triggering a full-scale rescue operation.

Authorities said they were not immediately notified because the miners were operating illegally, and local miners and residents initially tried to pump water from the site themselves before the situation became unmanageable.

The 325 rescue personnel have been facing challenging conditions, with narrow excavation pits about 100 metres (330 feet) deep, minimal lighting and slippery terrain conditions, Desiana said.

“The depth of the shaft, narrow ⁠access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely,” Desiana explained. “All efforts are made by taking into account field conditions and prioritising the safety of personnel involved in SAR (search and rescue) operations,” she added.

Eleven miners were able to leave safely before water flooded the shafts on Monday, West Java police spokesperson Hendra Rochmawan said.

The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital, Jakarta, where state miner ⁠Antam runs gold-mining operations.

Small-scale and unauthorised mining often leads to accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate .

articles.title: DR Congo Ebola cases surpass 12,000 as fighting disrupts response in east
articles.summary: Authorities struggle to contain country’s worst Ebola outbreak, as fighting in east displaces health workers, civilians.
articles.body:
The number of confirmed ‌Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 12,000, government data shows, as escalating fighting in the east disrupts efforts to contain the country’s deadliest outbreak on record.

Ebola response workers have been forced to leave affected areas amid worsening violence in the eastern DRC, health officials and humanitarian workers said on Wednesday.

Clashes in Ituri province have intensified in recent days between the Congolese army and fighters from the Convention for the ⁠Popular Revolution (CRP), displacing civilians, the United Nations mission said in a statement.

Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization’s Ebola incident manager, said about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia after three days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

“They were caught really in the crossfire, very intense fighting, and we managed to evacuate them,” Smallwood said.

The CRP is led by Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 ⁠of conscripting child soldiers. The group declared a unilateral ceasefire in May, but fighting has continued.

It is one of more than 100 armed groups in the eastern DRC, where conflict has disrupted efforts to contain the country’s worst Ebola outbreak on record.

At least 12,021 infections have been confirmed, including 5,904 deaths, government data showed on Thursday.

The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, was declared in mid-May in Ituri province in the northeastern DRC. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for this species.

Delayed detection, conflict, and strained health services have accelerated the spread of infections, with cases reported in eight of the DRC’s 26 provinces.

Sandrine Buju, a humanitarian worker involved in the Ebola response, said her team came under gunfire on Monday while returning to Bunia after training community volunteers.

“We were surprised by gunfire about 15 metres (50ft) from where we were,” she told The Associated Press news agency. “I was very frightened.”

The driver immediately turned around, and the team sought protection at a UN peacekeeping base, Buju said. Peacekeepers later escorted them through two areas of fighting towards Bunia.

articles.title: Guinea orders mass clean-up in Conakry months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
articles.summary: The capital's main rubbish dump has been closed since the disaster, leading to rubbish piling up in the streets.
articles.body:
Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.

Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.

In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.

The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.

At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.

He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.

The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.

"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.

"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.

He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.

Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.

The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.

The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.

According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

articles.title: Government preparing to publish more Lord Mandelson papers
articles.summary: The peer was sacked as UK ambassador to the US due to his links with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
articles.body:
Further documents relating to the appointment of Lord Mandelson as US ambassador are expected to be published by the government later today.

Some documents were published earlier this year after MPs voted to compel the government to release them, but others were withheld at the request of the Metropolitan Police, who are investigating the former ambassador.

The Met has since informed the government the documents can be published without prejudicing their investigation.

Lord Mandelson was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. He has repeatedly let it be known he believes he has not acted criminally, did not act for personal gain and is cooperating with the police.

The former Labour peer became the British ambassador to the US in February 2025.

But he was sacked in September of that year after Downing Street said new information about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein had emerged.

After his sacking, the government - then led by Sir Keir Starmer - was heavily criticised for giving Lord Mandelson the job and in February MPs voted to force the government to publish papers relating to his appointment.

In March, the first batch of files - running to 147 pages - was released. The documents showed Sir Keir was warned that Lord Mandelson's relationship with Epstein posed a "reputational risk" before he was confirmed as US ambassador.

More documents were published in June and they revealed messages between Lord Mandelson and ministers strongly criticising Sir Keir. The 1,500 pages covered communications about Lord Mandelson's appointment to the post.

The Cabinet Office earlier this month confirmed it was preparing to publish more documents. This led to the Conservatives warning that "we still haven't got to the bottom of the Mandelson scandal".

A Met Police spokesperson said: "Our investigation into alleged misconduct in public office is ongoing."

articles.title: Fuel tanker crash ignites a massive fire on a highway surrounding Cairo, killing at least 31 people
articles.summary: A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.
articles.body: A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said. The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the Health Ministry. The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighborhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the Health Ministry. At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb. Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars. “It was a huge fire, the cars got stuck together because of the fire,” he told the AP, describing the fear and panic that followed. “It was a shocking scene.” Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The Public Prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were underway to identify the victims. Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene himself. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. Initial statements said 25 people were injured, but that figure was later revised to 21. Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes. In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a massive multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.
