articles.title: A man bought a Washington property and registered it in sister's name to shield it from his wife; years later, after he developed Alzheimer's, his children challenged their aunt's ownership in court
articles.summary: A family property arrangement made nearly three decades ago has turned into a legal battle between a brother's children and their aunt in Washington, DC.
articles.body: A family property arrangement made nearly three decades ago has turned into a legal battle between a brother's children and their aunt in Washington, DC. In 1999, Sahr L. Bockai Sr. purchased a property in the city's Anacostia neighbourhood but had it registered in his sister Janet Finda Ahmadu's name. He reportedly wanted to protect the asset from his estranged wife amid marital difficulties. Bockai paid the deposit, repaid the mortgage and managed the property for years, while Ahmadu maintained that it had been given to her as a gift. The dispute escalated after Bockai developed Alzheimer's disease, prompting his children to challenge their aunt's ownership in court.Man put Washington property in sister's name to shield it from wifeBockai purchased the property at 1932 Martin Luther King Jr Avenue Southeast in 1999, intending to open a pharmacy. He paid a $20,000 deposit, while a mortgage of $180,000 was taken out to finance the purchase. The deed, however, was registered in Ahmadu's name, with the mortgage arranged using her power of attorney.According to testimony from Bockai's former accountant, he had chosen this arrangement because he was separated from his wife and wanted to prevent her from claiming the property during a potential divorce. He intended to have the property transferred into his own name later for a nominal amount.Ahmadu disputed this account. She said her brother had gifted her the property in gratitude for supporting him after he immigrated to the US and while he was qualifying to work as a pharmacist.Brother managed the property for nearly two decadesAlthough Ahmadu was named on the deed, Bockai handled the property's day-to-day affairs. He operated a pharmacy there, paid the mortgage, taxes and other expenses, arranged improvements and collected rent from tenants.Ahmadu said she had allowed him to manage the property because she was not in a position to do so herself. She also gave him power of attorney and did not charge him rent for using the premises. According to her account, he could use the property's proceeds for improvements and send any remaining money to her to support relatives in Sierra Leone.The siblings apparently had no significant disagreements over the arrangement for years. Their relationship with regard to the property came under strain only towards the end of the 2010s.Alzheimer's diagnosis brought the ownership dispute into focusBockai developed Alzheimer's disease in the late 2010s. His children were subsequently appointed as his guardians following proceedings in Maryland.The children then challenged Ahmadu's ownership, arguing that their father had been the actual owner and that she was taking advantage of his deteriorating mental condition. They maintained that he had paid for and controlled the property, despite the deed being in his sister's name.During the proceedings, evidence was also presented about Bockai's use of relatives' names in other property transactions. In one instance, he had purchased a property in his son's name without initially informing him. After discovering the arrangement, the son transferred the property to his father without receiving payment. Bockai had also used his daughter's name for another property, which she regarded as belonging to him.Lower court recognised brother as the property's ownerAfter a three-day trial, a Washington, DC, Superior Court ruled in Bockai's favour. It concluded that he had acquired ownership through adverse possession, a legal principle under which someone may obtain rights over property after possessing it openly and continuously for a specified period.The court declared Bockai the sole legal and equitable owner of the property. It also ordered Ahmadu to reimburse him for legal costs and expenses.Ahmadu challenged the decision, arguing that her brother's management of the property had taken place with her permission and could not establish adverse possession.Appeals court overturns adverse possession rulingOn September 3, 2026, the District of Columbia Court of Appeals overturned the lower court's adverse possession finding and set aside the order requiring Ahmadu to pay legal fees.Under Washington, DC, law, adverse possession requires someone to demonstrate actual, open, notorious, exclusive, continuous and hostile possession of a property for at least 15 years.The appeals court found that Bockai's management of the property had been authorised by Ahmadu through the power of attorney. She had not revoked that authority, and there was no evidence that he had told her he rejected her ownership. The court therefore concluded that his possession had not been established as hostile.The judges also noted that the siblings' relationship had apparently remained peaceful for years, with disagreements emerging only later.Ownership dispute returns to lower courtThe appeals court's decision did not establish Ahmadu as the property's rightful owner. Instead, it sent the case back to the lower court to consider other possible legal claims.These include whether Bockai could seek compensation for the money he invested in the property, including the initial deposit and mortgage repayments. The court also left open the possibility of considering claims such as unjust enrichment or a constructive trust.The case will therefore return to the lower court, where the competing claims over the property and the financial contributions made by Bockai will be examined further.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nine injured in explosion at oil facility in Thailand’s Bangkok
articles.summary: Bangchak Corporation says preliminary investigation finds the incident occurred at the refinery’s hydrocracking unit.
articles.body:
An explosion and a fire at an oil facility in Bangkok has injured at least nine people, authorities said, as residents in the surrounding area were urged to evacuate their homes.

Thailand’s Bangchak Corp said on Thursday it has shut down all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery following a fire.

At least nine people were injured in the fire, four of those seriously, according to Bangkok’s Erawan Emergency Medical Centre.

The sprawling site in eastern Bangkok is run by Thai energy conglomerate Bangchak Corporation. Based on a preliminary investigation, the incident occurred at the refinery’s hydrocracking unit, the company said.

The company said the Pollution Control Department conducted air quality measurements within a 3-4 km radius of the refinery and confirmed that the air quality was within normal ranges.

Thailand’s Energy minister Akanat Promphan, visiting the scene, told reporters it appeared the fire broke out at a distillation tower, “which was at least 100 metres (330 feet) away from the oil depot”, limiting the damage.

Videos posted on social media showed flames rising high above the site in eastern Bangkok, and thick black smoke sweeping across the Thai capital’s skyline.

“For their own safety, members of the public in the vicinity are urged to evacuate the area immediately,” the Bangna District Office said in a statement on its Facebook page.

Al Jazeera’s Tony Cheng, reporting from Chiang Mai, said the explosion was heard at about 3pm local time (08:00 GMT). The oil facility is “fairly close to the city centre, but still in a remote area that has a lot of industrial offices, warehouses, and near to Bangkok’s main port”, he said.

“The authorities say the fire was brought under control,” Cheng said, adding that “the highway and most of the major traffic routes in that area are still operational.”

Cheng said the large plume of black smoke would have pushed the authorities to share the evacuation warning. “We have seen industrial accidents in that area in the past couple of years,” he added.

“It serves not just Bangkok, but a large part of central Thailand. Most of the oil imports coming into this part of Thailand go here,” he added. “We don’t know at this stage the full extent of the damage, but one would imagine that it is quite considerable.”

Bangchak Corporation’s website describes the site as a “modern complex refinery with a maximum capacity of 120,000 barrels per day”.

An explosion occurred at the refinery in July 2012 — owned by then Bangchak Petroleum, which became the Bangchak Corporation — triggering a massive fire but no reported injuries.

At the time, there were questions asked about why such a large facility was located in what is now a residential area of Bangkok.

articles.title: Israel kills nine in Gaza, including Hamas-appointed deputy education minister, officials say
articles.summary: Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least nine Palestinians in Gaza overnight, medics said, including the Hamas-appointed deputy minister of education, in a third consecutive night of air attacks despite a one-year-old ceasefire.
articles.body: Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least nine Palestinians in Gaza overnight, medics said, including the Hamas-appointed deputy minister of education, in a third consecutive night of air attacks despite a one-year-old ceasefire. Medics said an Israeli airstrike hit an apartment in Deir Al-Balah, in central Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing Khaled Abu Nada, the deputy Gaza education minister, and his wife. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the attack was one of a series of targeted killings carried out recently against members and senior officials in Hamas, adding that Israel has killed about 80 Hamas militants in the past month. “No terrorist is immune, and no one in the Hamas leadership will manage to evade us,” Netanyahu said. Abu Nada was the third senior Hamas official Israel has killed since Tuesday, after two senior security officials. The Israeli military said Abu Nada oversaw Hamas’ economic portfolio and managed its banking and investment network, directing funds toward militant activities and force buildup. The military said his death may weaken the group’s ability to sustain its finances and support its military capabilities. Hamas confirmed the death but had no immediate comment on the allegations about his role. It said Israel’s targeting of academics and civilian figures was a “heinous crime.” Hamas said the continued policy of “assassination” violates the Gaza ceasefire agreement and international law, holding US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace politically and morally responsible for failing to stop the attacks and for providing cover that it said encouraged further killings and attacks on civilians. Two other separate airstrikes killed six people in Tuffah neighbourhood and Beach refugee camp overnight in Gaza City, medics added. Later on Thursday, medics said Israeli gunfire killed a 62-year-old man in eastern Bureij refugee camp. The Israeli military didn’t immediately comment on those seven reported deaths. Israel has continued to carry out attacks that it says target Hamas but which have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by Trump, has not halted the violence or secured Hamas’ disarmament. At least 1,600 Palestinians and 5 ​Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire was agreed in October 2025, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies. Israeli ​troops now ⁠control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza’s coast. Israel’s assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a ⁠hunger ​crisis, internally displaced Gaza’s entire population and led to assessments of genocide ​from scholars and a United Nations inquiry. Israel has denied the allegations of genocide, saying it acted in self-defense after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than ​250 hostages in an attack on Israel in October 2023.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un presses for wider nuclear deployment on facility tour
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said his country should focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains and that its nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded, state media KCNA reported on Thursday.
articles.body: SEOUL — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un said his country should focus on deploying tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains and that its nuclear material production capacity was being systematically expanded, state media KCNA reported on Thursday. Kim, during an inspection on Wednesday of nuclear material production and weapons research facilities, also said North Korea’s status as a nuclear weapons state was “absolutely inviolable”. KCNA did not identify the facilities or their locations. “Our nuclear capability is now a reality,” KCNA quoted Kim as saying. Kim said North Korea should “focus on utilising tactical nuclear weapons across multiple domains for different missions” and called recent achievements in nuclear weapons production a major success. The tour of facilities underscores Pyongyang’s push to expand and diversify its nuclear arsenal in defiance of calls for denuclearisation, as questions persist over prospects for renewed dialogue with the United States. Photographs released by KCNA showed Kim and officials inspecting objects that analysts said looked like gas centrifuges, used to enrich uranium, and miniaturised, standardised tactical nuclear warheads such as the Hwasan-31. Tactical nuclear weapons are generally lower-yield warheads meant for battlefield use, unlike strategic weapons intended for longer-range strikes. In 2023, KCNA published images of what it called the Hwasan-31 tactical nuclear warhead, saying it could be fitted to delivery systems, including short-range missiles. KCNA said Kim also toured a “nuclear-powered equipment production base,” which analysts said may be the first showing of equipment for a naval nuclear reactor programme. Ankit Panda, an analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote that the images from the base, which he described as a naval reactor facility, were “a very notable disclosure.” Shin Jong-woo, secretary-general of the Korea Defence and Security Forum, said the facility was believed to be producing submarine reactors and parts, adding that the pictured equipment could be used for a nuclear-powered submarine planned for next year. Kim also said any attempt to deny North Korea’s nuclear status would be regarded as “an open declaration of war”. “Our possession of nuclear weapons is an absolutely irreversible choice as long as malicious forces exist that use nuclear weapons as a means of achieving hegemony,” Kim said. Kim justified the buildup by citing growing nuclear threats from the United States and its allies. The United States had “incited its vassal states” near North Korea to acquire nuclear-powered submarines by introducing the “dangerous precedent of nuclear proliferation through AUKUS to Northeast Asia,” he said, referring to the security pact also involving Britain and Australia. He also accused Washington of building a “nuclear military alliance system” by trying to share and use nuclear weapons with its allies. South Korea is pursuing nuclear-powered submarines after US President Donald Trump approved the plan in October last year. South Korea’s Defence Ministry said its military was taking seriously North Korea’s stated intent to expand tactical nuclear weapons and urged Pyongyang to “immediately stop trying to justify its nuclear development” and implement UN Security Council resolutions. Seoul’s military would strengthen deterrence through consultations with the US and upgrade its response to nuclear threats, it said. Analysts said the visit carried a message for Washington amid speculation about US-North Korea contact. “This is not so much North Korea permanently closing the door to dialogue with the United States as a strategy of raising the bar: ‘denuclearisation talks’ are over, and if talks open in future, it will deal only on a ‘nuclear state versus nuclear state’ basis,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University. Shin said Kim’s reference to “multiple domains” could signal targets beyond the Korean peninsula, including the US mainland. North Korea has conducted six nuclear tests since 2006, with its last and most powerful test in 2017. South Korea’s defence minister said in August that Pyongyang was believed to possess between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads, but said the estimate came from private research organisations and could not be officially confirmed.

articles.title: How Hong Kong is marking the anniversary of its deadly fire amid police warnings
articles.summary: Hong Kong residents on Thursday remembered the victims of the city’s deadliest fire in decades by offering flowers and prayers days after the government warned them to be cautious about commemorative activities and to avoid being exploited by people it said had ulterior motives.
articles.body: HONG KONG — Hong Kong residents on Thursday remembered the victims of the city’s deadliest fire in decades by offering flowers and prayers days after the government warned them to be cautious about commemorative activities and to avoid being exploited by people it said had ulterior motives. The blaze engulfed seven high-rise buildings in Wang Fuk Court on Nov. 26, 2025, killing 168 people and displacing thousands of others in a disaster unimaginable in the wealthy financial hub known for its safety and modernity. A year on, many fire survivors were still grieving their losses despite life pushing them forward to adjust to their temporary housing, arrange funerals for their loved ones, clean up their belongings retrieved from charred homes and decide on resettlement plans. At a park near the apartment complex in Tai Po in the north of Hong Kong, a steady stream of residents laid flowers, snacks and toys to pay tribute. Some returned to the familiar area and gazed at their old homes. Others were seen crying. Survivor YN Chi still remembers her escape from the complex a year ago, saying she wouldn’t be alive if she had left five minutes later. She feels frightened when she thinks about it. “My greatest wish is to deliver the truth for those 168 victims,” she said. “They are truly innocent. It’s tragic.” Beijing warns of attempts to stir up chaos The tragedy is a sensitive issue in the Chinese territory, and not everyone feels free to speak about it. As the first anniversary approached, Hong Kong’s No. 2 official, Eric Chan, said last Friday that the government would allow all lawful commemorations but reminded residents to choose carefully what to take part in and not to be exploited by others to engage in disruptive acts. Without identifying anyone, he said some people spoke plainly online that they hoped to use this opportunity to organize people to come out or carry out acts of disruption. Echoing that, China’s Hong Kong and Macao Affairs Office on Tuesday urged vigilance against attempts to “use the disaster to stir up chaos.” It said the government’s response demonstrated its decisive action in advancing reforms with efficiency and pragmatism. Many residents have gradually emerged from the shadow of the tragedy and are grateful to the government and society, it added. But Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, said the city government responded to the fire “by using Beijing’s tactics of shutting out the voices of the victims and promising an elusive accountability.” Kai Chou, who studies in Tai Po, saw the flames from afar when the blaze broke out and, as a Hong Konger, he felt compelled to commemorate the victims in a tragedy that involved human-made mistakes. He said it was needless for the government to urge residents to guard against those with ulterior motives and questioned if it was treating residents as “terrorists.” “You made mistakes too, and yet even when we’re just trying to mourn, you still have to say things like this,” the 18-year-old Chou said. Grace Chan, a non-Tai Po resident who offered a flower, told reporters with tears in her eyes that Hong Kong has changed and she could not digest it. Hong Kong Journalists Association Chairperson Selina Cheng noted on Threads Wednesday that local journalists faced challenges in their anniversary coverage, saying a local television station had not broadcast its own report. On the eve of the anniversary, the Hong Kong office of China’s Foreign Ministry emailed foreign news outlets, including The Associated Press, to provide information about the aftermath of the fire for reference, saying the government was taking seriously the weak links in building maintenance and fire safety regulations exposed by the fire, and that it was committed to pursuing reform and investigations. Religious commemorations are held Beyond Tai Po, religious commemorations were held across the city, including a Wednesday Mass that drew hundreds, including bereaved families. At a cathedral in Hong Kong’s downtown, the names of the 168 victims were read out one by one. Jenny Lam, a pastor who lost three family members in the fire, said that on many sleepless nights, she thought about how those who remain should live on. She later realized they needed to live well. “It’s not about forgetting our pain,” she said. “But rather ... to continue experiencing the beauty of this world on their behalf.” Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the blaze, said she pondered where the victims lived and how their families would feel when she heard their names. Lo had anticipated the government would hold commemoration activities, saying its apology was already late and doing so would show it was truly walking alongside them. “There was disappointment, but I won’t place any expectations on it anymore,” Lo said. Eric Chan, the official, earlier told a radio show that the authorities did not hold commemorations because other similar activities were already being organized. An investigation found the blaze was likely caused by a lit cigarette and spread rapidly through non-fire-retardant scaffolding material. The report blamed faults in the complex’s renovation work and oversight deficiencies by several government departments. Just a month ago, Hong Kong leader John Lee and officials bowed in apology, while his housing minister resigned. Da Chung, a former Wang Fuk Court resident who attended the Mass, said that she was learning to make peace with it, but it was not easy for everyone. She could feel the sadness of those who lost their families during the event. “Their grief hangs in the air,” she said.

articles.title: Iqbal in space: Urdu poet’s verses unite India, Pakistan beyond Earth
articles.summary: Pakistan’s first astronaut recited Iqbal on board China’s space station, echoing two earlier encounters in orbit.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – Floating inside China’s Tiangong space station on Wednesday, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali turned to a poet from home.

Wearing a blue flight suit bearing the green-and-white Pakistani flag and surrounded by five Chinese crewmates, Pakistan’s first astronaut recited a couplet by Muhammad Iqbal, the country’s national poet.

“Sitaron se aage jahan aur bhi hain / abhi ishq ke imtihan aur bhi hain,” Ali said.

He paused briefly between the two lines before repeating the opening phrase and completing the verse, trying to steady himself as he floated.

He then smoothly switched to Mandarin, translating the couplet’s meaning to his Chinese crewmates.

“Countless worlds lie beyond the stars, and countless trials are still ahead,” he said.

As he finished with a thank-you and a smile, the crew broke into applause and cheers before coming together for midair hugs and laughter.

But this was not the first time Iqbal’s poetry had travelled from Earth into orbit.

The first such exchange took place in 1984, when Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian in space, invoked the poet’s words while responding to then Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi’s question about how India looked from above.

In 1997, another Indian-born astronaut, Kalpana Chawla, heard Iqbal’s poetry quoted by then-Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral during a conversation from orbit. Gujral recited the opening line of the same couplet Ali would read to his Chinese crewmates decades later.

Iqbal was a poet, philosopher and political thinker whose ideas helped shape Muslim politics in South Asia in the early 20th century.

Born on November 9, 1877, in Sialkot in what was then British India, he studied in Lahore, England, and Germany; qualified in law; and earned a doctorate in philosophy.

Across South Asia, he is still widely known as Allama, meaning the learned one.

He wrote primarily in Persian and Urdu. His Persian poetry earned him a lasting following in Iran, as well, where he is known as Iqbal-e-Lahori, or Iqbal of Lahore.

In 1930, while presiding over the annual session of the All-India Muslim League in Allahabad, he proposed that Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Balochistan be brought together in a single self-governing state, within or outside the British Empire.

Although he did not use the word “Pakistan” in his address, his proposal came to be regarded as the intellectual idea that eventually led to the country’s creation. In Pakistan, he is often described as the man who dreamed of the country.

Iqbal died in Lahore on April 21, 1938, nine years before Partition led to the creation of Pakistan in 1947.

When did India’s first astronaut quote him?

Rakesh Sharma, a squadron leader in the Indian Air Force, flew on board the Soviet Soyuz T-11 mission on April 3, 1984. He spent nearly eight days on board the Salyut 7 space station.

That month, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi spoke to him during a televised conversation.

“Upar se Bharat kaisa dikhta hai aapko?” she asked. (How does India look to you from up there?)

“Ji, main baghair kisi jhijhak ke keh sakta hoon ke sare jahan se achha,” Sharma replied. (I can say without any hesitation, better than the whole world.)

His response referred to Iqbal’s famous poem, Tarana-e-Hindi, written in 1904, which includes the line “Sare jahan se achha, Hindustan hamara” (Better than the whole world, our India).

Later rendered as a song, Sare jahan se achcha was one of the anthems of India’s independence struggle. It remains one of India’s most popular patriotic songs, and the Indian Army band frequently performs it on major occasions.

When did India’s prime minister cite Iqbal during a space mission?

Chawla, born in the Indian state of Haryana, made her first spaceflight on board the US space shuttle Columbia, which launched on November 19, 1997.

During her next space visit in 2003, she died along with her crewmates when the shuttle broke apart during its return to Earth.

Gujral, who was born in Jhelum, in what is now Pakistan, was fluent in Urdu and had a fondness for poetry. During a conversation with Chawla on board the 1997 shuttle journey, he turned to Iqbal.

“There is a saying by one of our poets who’s very well known in the subcontinent, Iqbal.”

He then recited the opening line of the same couplet that Ali would quote nearly three decades later.

“There are worlds beyond stars. And now you have seen them. How do you feel about them?” he asked.

“It’s a very special feeling … What you are saying does become very literal,” Chawla replied.

“It’s a dome of a dark sky and stars everywhere,” she said. “And it is very much like a storybook.”

Along with Pakistan’s founder, Muhammad Ali Jinnah (left), Allama Iqbal (right) remains the other primary figure credited with creating Pakistan in August 1947. He is regarded as the country’s national poet and the man who dreamed up the idea of Pakistan [File: Rahat Dar/EPA]

NASA administrator Bill Nelson poses for a picture with former Indian Astronaut Rakesh Sharma – and a cutout of Sharma – during a conversation with NASA and ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation) at VITM Auditorium, in Bengaluru, India, on November 29, 2023 [Nivedita Bhattacharjee/Reuters]

articles.title: Thanksgiving reminds us that gratitude, not grievance, carries a nation through
articles.summary: From a 1541 Texas barbecue to the 1621 Mayflower feast, America's multiple "first Thanksgivings" reveal how gratitude united colonists and tribes alike.
articles.body: This year, Thanksgiving takes place during America’s celebratory 250th year. Yet it also arrives amid a culture clash. Earlier in 2026, canceling Thanksgiving became a political controversy when Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong struggled to defend a past social media screed. "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," Hong wrote in a now-deleted 2020 post. Hong, who lost her election, failed to appreciate a crucial fact about the 1621 Thanksgiving. Giving thanks to God the Creator was a shared value between the 53 Mayflower passengers and the 90 Wampanoags when they celebrated a three-day feast in Massachusetts in 1621. Both sides had survived catastrophic losses. One lost nearly half of its members to poor food and shelter, while the other had suffered from a deadly disease. AS AMERICA MARKS 250 YEARS, OUR GREATEST CHAPTERS ARE STILL AHEAD OF US The takeaway is that giving thanks despite their suffering is what brought these different groups together. My new book, "A Great and Grateful Nation: From Grievance to Gratitude," reveals the truth about America’s multiple "first Thanksgivings" between colonists and tribes. It also reveals America’s history of embracing gratitude amid grievances. Two years earlier, in 1619, Virginians toasted their survival upon arrival in the first English Thanksgiving in America. Not to be outdone, Florida’s shores bore thankfulness lore through two Thanksgivings even earlier in the 1560s: one by Spanish Catholics and the Seloy, and the other by French Protestants and the Timucua. Texas staked the earliest claim to Thanksgiving fame. In 1541, Spanish explorers held a Thanksgiving Mass and feasted on buffalo with the Teyas. Hence, the first European Thanksgiving in America wasn’t a turkey dinner, but a Texas barbecue. Why is the 1621 Massachusetts event the ancestor of our Thanksgiving tradition? Unlike these other "firsts," Thanksgiving became a yearly occurrence in New England. The point isn’t so much about who was first—Native tribes had given ceremonial thanks to the Creator for centuries. The point is that despite different theologies, gratitude to God is a shared value that transcends ethnicities. The other takeaway is that gratefulness isn’t about nostalgia; it’s about perspective. This year, millions have celebrated America’s 250th anniversary through numerous events. During the American Revolution, however, Thanksgiving wasn’t confined to a Thursday in November. Our founders frequently set aside days of gratitude while enduring countless grievances against England. GEORGE WASHINGTON'S REMARKABLE PRAYER FOR AMERICA STILL RESONATES 250 YEARS LATER For example, John and Abigail Adams observed two Thanksgivings close together. In November 1765, over Thanksgiving dinner at her parents’ house, they agonized over the controversial Stamp Act, which imposed a tax on paper goods. Then, they were so overjoyed when the king repealed the Stamp Act that they and their fellow Massachusettsans celebrated a Thanksgiving in July 1766. The relief was short-lived. The king’s tyranny continued through military occupations, censorship, corrupt courts, taxation without representation and dissolved legislatures. Despite their grievances, gratitude persisted. While in Cambridge in 1775, Gen. George Washington was so intrigued by Massachusetts’ tradition that he wrote the word "thanksgiving" for the first time in his general orders, calling for his men to join in. This was the army’s first Thanksgiving. MIKE PENCE: THE NEXT GENERATION NEEDS FAITH IN GOD AND CONFIDENCE IN THE AMERICAN IDEAL Two years later, after the victorious Battle of Saratoga in New York, the Continental Congress called on all Americans to observe a day of thanks in December 1777. A few months later, in May 1778, when Washington learned that France had become America’s ally, he was so thrilled that he set aside a day for his men to celebrate and give thanks. The army soon rejoiced again with a day of thanks following the Battle of Monmouth in June 1778. Washington’s final victory against the British at Yorktown in October 1781 led Congress to celebrate with a national day to "thankfully acknowledge the interpositions of his Providence." They also sent Washington a thank-you note for winning the war. WHAT WILL WE LEAVE OUR CHILDREN? THE AMERICAN DREAM DEMANDS MORE THAN COMFORT Americans didn’t give thanks in 1781 because every problem was solved. Rather, gratitude helped them persevere through their hardships to obtain victory. They refused to let their grievances be the final lens through which they viewed their history, neighbors, country and God’s mercies. President Abraham Lincoln did the same thing during the Civil War. It’s not an accident that Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation to set the nation on the path toward abolishing slavery in the same year—1863—that he made Thanksgiving a national holiday for all the states. He was projecting the direction of where he wanted America to go. Today, in America’s 250th year, some still elevate grievance over gratitude, as Hong’s "cancel Thanksgiving" tweet showed. Despite this, if we are willing, gratitude continues to offer a better path: one that celebrates the great in America’s history, forgives injustices, learns from past sins and prepares the next generation to preserve liberty. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Forgiveness is not historical amnesia, nor is it a declaration that evil was good. Gratitude gives Americans moral room to acknowledge slavery, discrimination and corruption while also celebrating the Declaration of Independence, Constitution, Bill of Rights, emancipation and civil rights as inheritances of liberty requiring our stewardship. America became a great nation because Americans were grateful along the way. So, how can we give thanks for our nation this Thanksgiving in America’s 250th year? One suggestion is to take five minutes and make a national gratitude list. Write down one freedom we regularly use, one sacrifice that secured it, and one responsibility we have because of it. For example, freedom of speech can lead us to use words truthfully, while freedom of religion can lead us to both practice our faith and respect others’ consciences. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP America’s survival and revival depend on each generation choosing unifying gratitude over unforgiven grievance. Gratefulness is the nation’s renewable fuel. Thanksgiving is our annual maintenance checkup, if we choose to embrace it. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM JANE HAMPTON COOK

articles.title: Trump’s midterms debacle hasn’t dimmed his designs on Cuba. Or those of ‘President’ Rubio
articles.summary: The historic drubbing US President Donald Trump received in the US midterm elections apparently has not dimmed the enthusiasm he feels for one of his most high-risk foreign policy goals: “Taking Cuba,” as he put it.
articles.body: The historic drubbing US President Donald Trump received in the US midterm elections apparently has not dimmed the enthusiasm he feels for one of his most high-risk foreign policy goals: “Taking Cuba,” as he put it earlier this year. “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday. Trump said he would consider using military action to topple the island’s leadership. Even as voters in the midterms widely rejected Trump’s war in Iran, the US president suggests he still has the communist-run island just 90 miles from Florida in his crosshairs. The comments further escalated tensions with Cuba, which for months has been readying soldiers and civilian militias for a possible US invasion. “Cuba does not attack or threaten any nation,” responded Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel on X, “But we will reject any attempt at foreign military aggression and we are preparing for that threat.” For nearly a year, Trump has ratcheted up sanctions on the island — including an oil embargo — while alternatively portraying Cuba as both a failed state and grave threat to US national security. A US State Department report in July titled “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism” ominously accused Havana of “persuading the children of the West to turn against their own inheritance” and laid out what many observers read as the case for regime change on the island. Trump has wavered on whether the US will follow through on military action to force Cuba’s government from power, saying the country’s economy is already collapsing and that he may place a US aircraft carrier off the island’s coast before sending US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to Havana to hammer out a deal literally at gunpoint. Rubio, a Cuban-American and staunch critic of the Cuban government, has made clear that there needs to be new leadership on the island and that under US law, “regime change” is a condition for economic sanctions to be lifted. “You cannot change the economic trajectory of Cuba as long as the people who are in charge of it now are in charge of it,” Rubio told Fox News in May. “I don’t think we’re going to be able to change the trajectory of Cuba as long as these people are in charge in that regime.” In several tense meetings in 2026, US officials told Cuban counterparts they needed to liberalize the island’s economic and political models and end cooperation with US adversaries or face the consequences. The May indictment of former Cuban President Raul Castro — who is 95 but still wields enormous power on the island — just months after the US capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro — drove home those warnings. And while the US still technically maintains diplomatic relations with Cuba, for months the Trump administration has referred to Cuba’s government as “an illegitimate regime.” The impasse boiled over into a shouting match at the UN last month, as Cuba’s Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla tried to interrupt US Ambassador Mike Waltz from giving a speech lambasting what he called Cuban leaders’ corruption and incompetence. A Cuban diplomat was later expelled for appearing to shove a US official. Privately, Cuban officials expressed hopes that a rout for Trump in the midterm elections and US voters’ apathy toward military interventions would cool the administration’s imperial designs on the island. The electoral rout came but there appears to be little reprieve in store for the beleaguered island nation during Trump’s remaining time in office. A US official, who did not want to be named, told CNN that Washington still expects “the regime to collapse” and that the midterms fiasco will not lead to any softening of the administration’s policy towards Cuba Having resisted US pressure for nearly 70 years, Cuba does not appear to be caving now. As grim as life has become for Cubans — blackouts now can last for days, medicine and food are increasingly scarce and the value of the Cuban peso is in a seemingly perpetual death spiral — the island’s government remains firmly in control. So far, the few talks that have taken place have yielded no tangible results and there is no sign that the administration has found, as US officials put it, “their Delcy” in the Cuban government, referring to Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s much more pliant successor in Venezuela. Trump’s prediction that the Cuba’s leadership will offer concessions to end the pressure campaign notwithstanding, there appears to be little chance of a diplomatic breakthrough. Cuban officials view any economic benefits of a deal to be a poisoned chalice. As one Cuban diplomat told me years ago, “We know that if the Americans are for it, we should be against it.” But Havana may be missing the opportunity to make a historic and lasting deal. “It’s ‘Nixon goes to China’,” said Ricardo Herrero, the executive director of the Cuba Study Group, a non-partisan organization focused on US-Cuba relations and the Cuban private sector. “You make the deal with your staunchest adversary on the other side, because that deal becomes untouchable. It’s going to come at a higher cost. But it has much greater longevity than any deal that you strike with the Democrats,” he said. Even if Rubio — widely viewed as the architect of Trump’s Cuba crackdown — were to leave the administration to mount his own bid for the presidency in 2028, any respite for Cuba would likely be short lived. As president, Rubio would undoubtably seek to finish what Trump started with Cuba.

articles.title: Meet the mastermind behind New York City's iconic Christmas light displays and holiday magic
articles.summary: Some of NYC's most popular Christmas decorations at Radio City Music Hall, Macy's and Bloomingdale's get help from one man and his crew every Christmas.
articles.body: While most of New York City is asleep, dedicated crews are racing against the clock to turn the Big Apple into a holiday wonderland. "I would say our average projects, probably about 30 people for a night or two," says American Christmas CEO Dan Casterella. Casterella is the man behind some of the most popular lighting displays in the tristate area. From Macy's, Bloomingdale’s, Saks Fifth Avenue and Radio City Music Hall to the FOX News Christmas Tree, Casterella and his team create the city's signature Christmas magic. FOX NEWS KICKS OFF HOLIDAY SEASON WITH CHRISTMAS TREE LIGHTING "It's like a once in a lifetime opportunity," Florida mom Kate Rankin tells FOX, "I feel like New York is… unlike anywhere else." "There’s a tradition of people visiting New York to see the holiday decorations," Casterella says, "I meet people all the time and even some of our clients kind of talk about how they used to do it with their parents when they were kids." Rankin shares the same story. "Growing up in Jersey, we did this as a kid," she tells FOX. "So we came all the time. And now that I live in Tampa, I try to bring my children up here so that they can see." REDDIT USERS SHARE WILDEST THINGS SEEN AT CHRISTMAS PARTIES To turn a building facade into a dazzling Christmas light show, Casterella says retailers reach out to his team months in advance—sometimes nearly a whole year. "I would say our entire company is 24 hours," Casterella tells FOX. "And that will continue for the next 10 to 15 days." American Christmas employs engineers, designers, welders and builders who piece each elaborate concept together. "We get into January and February, and we start designing and developing from there," Casterella says, "We go into engineering in March, and then in April, orders get placed." Casterella says that by the end of September, his crews are in full swing hanging up lights and building large-scale decorations. Once the season wraps up, Casterella says more than 2,500 truckloads of gear will have rolled into town, and more than 400 projects will be finished across the tristate area alone. His team also works nationwide, completing more than 800 projects bearing the American Christmas name by the end of the season. While losing hours of sleep and working grueling overnight shifts, Casterella says he has always had a passion for Christmas decorations, even telling FOX he would ask for decorations as Christmas gifts. "I've loved it since I was a kid. I was decorating homes for Christmas when I was a kid. That's how I made money in high school. And I was in college and started working here, and I never left," Casterella says. A popular stop decorated by Casterella and his team is Radio City Music Hall. The venue has been a client for over 20 years, and American Christmas crews continue to reimagine the 64-foot tree that is lit with 50,000 LEDs. As for the FOX News Christmas Tree, Casterella says it took his team 36 hours to build the frame and branches. The tree features 48,000 LEDs and thousands of ornaments wired into the branches to ensure wind or weather does not impact the display. articles.title: He built a shrine to China’s national liquor, with one catch: He’s allergic
articles.summary: As overseas collectors and auction houses develop a taste for Moutai, businessman Shi Yunding has one unusual obstacle.
articles.body: Like Superman collecting kryptonite or a vampire trading in garlic, Chinese-born businessman Shi Yunding is seemingly drawn to his mortal weakness. The 38-year-old is a major distributor of Moutai — a luxury variant of baijiu, China’s most popular liquor — in Singapore, where he has just opened a three-floor venue dedicated to the fiery spirit. He also owns around 1,000 of the distinctively sturdy, opaque bottles in his personal collection. None of them, however, are for drinking. In fact, he is allergic to alcohol. Consuming more than around 50 millimeters (a little more than three tablespoons) of baijiu triggers breathing difficulties from which he “usually needs three hours to recover,” Shi admitted while showing me around Moutai House, his new showroom-meets-bar-and-restaurant in downtown Singapore. “But after that, I’m OK.” Business interests aside, Shi’s collecting habit speaks to Moutai’s multifaceted role in Chinese culture. As well as being an effective route to intoxication (usually distilled to around 53% alcohol), it is both a status symbol and a luxury asset akin to whisky. Often described as China’s “national liquor,” Moutai is also a popular gift, the toast of choice for successful business deals and the unspoken currency of “guanxi” — the informal network of favors, influence and connections underpinning many social and commercial relationships. Shi began collecting the liquor more than a decade ago after receiving a bottle as a gift. In turn, he now frequently dips into his collection to find presents for friends and relatives (including his father-in-law), or as offerings at important social gatherings. He buys Moutai to commemorate important milestones, like his son’s birth, which he marked with a 2024 “Year of the Rabbit” edition. He also collects bottles nodding to his adopted home of Singapore, including rare examples featuring the country’s historical import labels. Unlike wines, whose value can fluctuate according to harvest quality, Moutai prices are very closely linked to scarcity. In China, the rarest vintages routinely sell at auction for over 1 million yuan ($150,000). The highest publicly documented auction price for a single bottle of Moutai is 10.7 million yuan (then about $1.7 million), fetched by a 1935 bottle in 2011. Shi’s current quest is acquiring bottles imported to Singapore during each year since 1965, when the country declared independence from Malaysia. He is now missing just five years, mostly from the 1970s, when the upheaval of then Chinese leader Mao Zedong’s chaotic and violent Cultural Revolution severely limited production, making bottles from the period among the most sought-after. “Sometimes it’s like a game of bingo,” Shi said of his mission to track down rare bottles. Occupying a century-old Art Deco building, his ambitious new venue is an ode to Moutai. Wall displays educate visitors on the drink’s history. A large showroom acts as a museum of sorts. Glass cases show off rare and limited-edition offerings. A decrepit looking 1953 bottle, on loan from a fellow collector and wrapped in crinkled brown paper, is supposedly worth around 1 million Singapore dollars ($777,000). Recent vintages retail at more budget-friendly — but by no means cheap — prices. Shi offered me glasses from 2024 and 2025 bottles, selling at 268 and 368 Singapore dollars ($207 and $285), respectively. Connoisseurs sometimes describe the potent clear spirit as possessing umami notes comparable to soy sauce or fermented beans, while some variants are fruitier, nuttier or more floral than others. For novices, quality may be best judged by how harsh (or not) it is on the throat, with price tags often correlating closely with how smoothly each sip slides down. Drink of Diplomacy Baijiu is a ubiquitous feature of Chinese life that cuts across social classes, geographies and price points. It is found everywhere from cheap convenience store fridges to the shelves of specialist luxury stores. Of the many varieties of baijiu, Moutai, which is typically distilled seven times during a year-long production process, is widely considered the most prestigious. Just as Champagne must originate from France’s Champagne region, Moutai must be produced in the town of the same name (now anglicized as Maotai), using water from the Chishui River. It is made by distilling sorghum and a wheat-based fermentation starter called “qu.” But while Moutai technically describes a style of baijiu brewed in the region for centuries, the term is today synonymous with one company: Kweichow Moutai. Worth an estimated 1.8 trillion yuan ($280 billion), it is the world’s most valuable spirits business, and China’s largest non-technology firm. The brand’s history is closely tied to that of China’s Communist Party. Mao famously passed through the town on his Long March expedition in the 1930s, with his Red Army troops instructed to refrain from disrupting the area’s baijiu production. Kweichow Moutai was subsequently formed as a state-owned merger between three neighboring distilleries in the early 1950s, shortly after Mao seized control of China in a bloody civil war. Widely reported to be Mao’s favorite drink, Moutai soon became the political lubricant of diplomacy and government banquets. Premier Zhou Enlai famously served it to Richard Nixon during the US president’s historic visit to China in 1972. (Nixon reportedly ignored an aide’s advice to avoid swallowing such a strong spirit during toasts, instead matching Zhou glass for glass.) At a state dinner two years later, US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger told future leader Deng Xiaoping: “I think if we drink enough Moutai, we can solve anything.” Today, the state retains a controlling stake in the company, though it has been publicly traded since 2001. And as Chinese consumers’ spending power has skyrocketed in recent decades, so too has Moutai’s status as a collector’s item. Zodiac animals are just some of the myriad limited-edition releases conjured up by Kweichow Moutai. Shi’s collection features ornate golden bottles commemorating China’s pavilion at the recent Osaka 2025 expo and numerous varieties of the “Discovery Collection,” designs themed around different countries, from France to Vietnam, that buyers can collect like Starbucks mugs. Yet, outside China no market has developed much of a taste for (or even been exposed to) Moutai, a drink sometimes nicknamed “firewater.” Despite exporting internationally for more than 70 years, domestic sales still account for more than 97% of Kweichow Moutai’s revenue. The company has stepped up efforts to expand its global footprint in recent years. With China’s Moutai market slowing significantly in the last decade — not least because of leader Xi Jinping’s campaigns against corruption and lavish government banquets, in a country where the line between “guanxi” and bribery can become easily blurred — overseas sales offer new avenues for growth. Going global Given that around 75% of its population is ethnically Chinese, Singapore was an obvious starting point. Enter Shi, who turned his personal interest in Moutai into a business by becoming one of the country’s official Kweichow Moutai distributors last year. His pivot to liquor was, partly, pragmatic: Having specialized in trading commodities like coal and bauxite, he needed to diversify as Singapore was “going green,” he said. But the collector also appears genuinely passionate about a drink he can only safely consume in tiny doses. Moutai House is entirely independent of Kweichow Moutai, though Shi said he has the firm’s blessing. At the venue’s rooftop bar, bartenders serve up eight signature cocktails made using Golden Prince, a more affordable, entry-level Moutai sub-brand (one wouldn’t, after all, make an Old Fashioned with a fine single malt). Classics like martinis and margaritas are also given extra kick with the spirit. Shi hopes to make Moutai accessible to people who may be entirely unfamiliar with baijiu, even in a country with close cultural ties to China. “We see more and more people willing to try Moutai,” he said. “Before they would have said, ‘This is too strong,’ or, ‘It smells weird,’ but today it’s different.” Convincing the world’s drinkers to embrace Moutai, or baijiu of any description, could be a decades-long mission for enthusiasts like Shi. International collectors and investors may need less persuasion. Once considered a niche luxury asset category, Moutai has enjoyed growing visibility at major Western auction houses in the last decade. A breakthrough moment came in 2021 when a crate of 24 bottles from 1974 smashed estimates to sell for £1 million ($1.3 million) at Sotheby’s in London. It was the highest price ever paid at an auction outside of China for a single lot of Moutai. Sealed in a crate with its original nails, the bottles’ value stemmed from their rarity, provenance and historical context. They featured Kweichow Moutai’s “Sunflower” export branding, which from 1969 briefly replaced its “Flying Fairy” brand due to fears that the latter’s imagery, based on China’s Mogao Caves, was ideologically inappropriate amid Mao’s campaign against the “four olds” (old ideas, culture, customs and habits). The 2021 sale was “definitely a landmark moment,” said Paul Wong, Sotheby’s head of wine and spirit for China, on a video call from Hong Kong. And while the auction house has never revealed the winning bidder’s identity (other than being an “Asian collector”), Wong added that he has seen “increasing appetite” among international collectors. At one of Sotheby’s recent Moutai auctions, more than a quarter of bidders came from outside Greater China, he said, with “particularly strong participation from Europe and Southeast Asia.” Easy to store and unlikely to spoil, the right vintages of baijiu, like certain whiskies, have the potential to appreciate significantly in value. But Moutai collectors arguably have more in common with wine enthusiasts. For one thing — and this makes Shi something of an outlier — they like to consume what they buy, Wong said. “They actually drink regularly and enjoy and share with friends,” he added. “Whereas I think with whiskies, especially on the very top end, people tend to treat the bottles as collectibles — trophy whiskies that they store and admire from afar.”

articles.title: ‘Proscribing free speech’: Why a Jewish group is challenging UK’s Hamas ban
articles.summary: The Jewish Network for Palestine says the complete ban on Hamas was being used to stifle free speech.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – The Jewish Network for Palestine (JNP) has filed an application to reverse the proscription of Hamas under Britain’s Terrorism Act, arguing that the ban is being used against its members and is hampering freedom of speech in the United Kingdom.

The JNP filed a formal de-proscription application on Thursday under Section 4 of the Terrorism Act, which oversees applications to remove a group from the UK’s list of banned organisations.

This follows the arrest of the 80-year-old son of Auschwitz survivors and the prosecution of a 72-year-old Jewish writer – both members of the JNP’s Steering Group – for pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist speech.

The JNP was founded in 2018 by British members of the United States organisation Jewish Voice for Peace, a group which aims to bring together Jews and non-Jews who support Palestine. It is one of 11 Jewish and Jewish-led organisations that form the UK’s Jewish bloc for Palestine, which is frequently present at protests against Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and pogroms in the West Bank.

According to the chair of the JNP, David Cannon, proscription of Hamas has made it near-impossible to openly discuss the events of October 7, 2023, when Hamas led an attack on villages and army outposts in southern Israel. In particular, the JNP says, it has been unable to talk publicly about false narratives that followed for fear of contravening the act.

“Now, all of these things needed to be discussed, but the UK government’s proscription of the political wing of Hamas has made referring to such evidence [of false reporting] risk the accusation of supporting Hamas, which is not what we’re saying. We’re saying that we want to discuss these issues,” he said.

In the days following October 7, when more than 1,000 people were killed, many stories about babies being killed by Hamas fighters and mass rapes were circulated in international media. There has been no evidence of these.

Cannon added that one of the group’s active members had resigned, fearing that what she could say would affect her immigration status if found to violate the act.

According to the application, the JNP has about 600 members and supporters.

The JNP’s application was filed five years to the day after the British government proscribed the whole of Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Hamas’s armed wing had been banned in 2001, but in 2021 the then-Home Secretary Priti Patel extended the ban to cover the whole political group, describing the organisation as “fundamentally and rabidly anti-Semitic” and arguing that the proscription was required to protect the Jewish community.

The government did not, however, explain how the proscription of Hamas would protect the Jewish community in the UK. Instead, the JNP argues that the designation has now been used against the Jewish community it was supposed to protect.

The group also argues that the continued proscription of Hamas in its entirety was a “disproportionate interference with the rights of JNP and its members” under the European Convention on Human Rights Articles 9, 10 and 11 on freedom of thought, expression and assembly, with the burden of the proscription falling on people in Britain.

Finally, they argue, Hamas has “no presence in the UK and has not been shown to pose a specific threat to it”.

“The less intrusive position that applied before November 2021 shows that proscription of the whole organisation is not necessary. On a proper application of the policy, and with the impact on JNP weighed, continued proscription is not justified,” the application stated.

Following the JNP’s application, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmoud has 90 days to consider it beginning the day after it is received. If it is refused, the group can appeal the decision.

Tony Greenstein, 72, an anti-Zionist writer and blogger and prominent member of the JNP, was prosecuted for publishing a blog on October 7, 2023, titled “Full Support for the Gaza Ghetto Uprising”, in which he evoked the Jewish Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in 1943.

While his post only mentioned Hamas in passing, in November 2024 Greenstein was charged under section 12 of the British Terrorism Act with inviting support for Hamas on the basis of one sentence in that blog and for writing “please share” on social media, promoting the piece.

After nearly three years and appearances in different courts, Greenstein was acquitted in August this year.

“If you can’t actually say what you think about an organisation without watching over your shoulder in case you’re contravening some law, then that’s chilling free speech, and that is the real issue,” Greenstein told Al Jazeera.

“That’s been made time and time again about the Terrorism Act. It’s really about clamping down on free speech,” he added.

During the criminal proceedings against him, five banks and building societies closed his accounts.

In Greenstein’s view, arresting Jews is not the best way to protect the Jewish community in the UK.

“It’s a very good way of protecting Zionism and the Zionists, and that is the difference,” he said. “The way they dress up their foreign policy choices is by saying they’re protecting a particular community. The reality is, of course, banning or proscribing Hamas has nothing at all to do with racist attacks against Jews, they’re completely separate phenomena.”

He added: “Hamas doesn’t operate in Britain. It never has operated in Britain …So how can we be at risk of being attacked by a group that doesn’t even exist here? It was about stopping people expressing an opinion on what’s happening in Gaza and in the occupied territories. That’s a very different thing.”

One of the founders of the JNP is Haim Bresheeth-Zabner, an 80-year-old Jewish-Israeli anti-Zionist filmmaker and film studies professor at the School of African and Oriental Studies (SOAS).

He was arrested and held for 13 hours in November 2024 immediately after he made a speech at a protest in Swiss Cottage, north London. It was part of wider protests held weekly by the International Jewish Anti-Zionist Network with the JNP’s involvement against the Israeli ambassador and the actions of the Israeli government in Gaza. In his speech, Bresheeth-Zabner said that the Israeli army “cannot fight the resistance” and “cannot win against Hamas … against Hezbollah …[or] against the Houthis”.

“They [the police] refused to discuss with me what I said that is considered applicable under the Terrorism Act. It took many hours of waiting in a very cold car park … I’m 80 … I have heart failure and cancer. So I wasn’t feeling all that well, but that didn’t make a difference. I also told them that I need to take my medications in the early evening, and they disregarded that,” Bresheeth-Zabner told Al Jazeera.

While he was not charged following his arrest, he said the ban has been used against people who want to speak up against the genocide in Gaza, making it impossible to criticise the Israeli army.

“This is a really odd situation where Britain, as a society, as a politicised society, as a country, as a regime, if you want, is not acting to uphold international law, and is proscribing our ability to speak against the genocide, to speak against Zionism, to speak against Israel. When we do that, we are arrested. We are charged,” he said.

“We’re [the JNP] supporting human rights, and human rights include the right to oppose a genocide, not just our right to oppose a genocide, but of course the rights of the victims of the genocide to resist it.”

articles.title: Highway explosion in Giza: How deadly are Egypt’s roads and railways?
articles.summary: Egypt has suffered another tragedy as a deadly road explosion kills 31 and injures dozens.
articles.body:
An explosion rocked a highway in Cairo when a fuel truck overturned and caught fire, killing at least 31 people on Wednesday.

Egypt’s public prosecutor has announced an investigation into the crash, and the Ministry of Health said it will continue to monitor the situation.

But Egypt is no stranger to deadly accidents on its roads, despite spending billions of dollars on its transportation systems.

So what exactly caused the explosion and how unsafe are Egypt’s roads?

On Wednesday evening, a fuel tanker travelling on a busy ring road in Giza’s Imbabah district, a highly populated, working-class part of the Greater Cairo area, crashed and exploded, causing a fire that killed at least 31 people and injured 21 others.

Local media have reported that the explosion happened after the truck driver swerved to avoid a high-voltage cable which fell in front of the vehicle.

Twenty-seven vehicles were caught up and burned in the accident, according to Egypt’s judicial office.

Thirty-nine ambulances were dispatched to the scene, taking the injured to nearby hospitals for treatment, the Health Ministry said.

Egypt’s public prosecutor announced that there will be an investigation into the crash and ordered DNA samples from victims.

Egypt, which has a population of around 120m, is known for its dangerous roads. It clocked up a total of 44,940 road deaths and 476,126 injuries between 2019 and 2025, according to the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS).

Last year, more than 5,800 road deaths and 84,000 road injuries were recorded by the agency, with pedestrians making up more than one-third of those killed.

Children under the age of 15 made up 1,580 of the deaths and 29,101 of the injured.

A World Bank report in 2020 found that the incidents occur because 97 percent of Cairo’s streets lack traffic lights and 78 percent of them have no clear pedestrian footpaths.

In 2025, there were 170 train incidents recorded, resulting in the deaths of 44 people and injuries to 215.

Earlier this month, at least seven people were killed and more than 125 others injured when a train backed into another, also in Giza, triggering calls for political accountability.

Egypt’s Ministry of Transport said that approximately $37bn was spent on transport investment between 2014 and 2024, but recurring incidents have raised questions about the effectiveness of this project.

The leader of the centrist Reform and Development Party’s parliamentary bloc, Irene Saeed, called for full financial transparency on how the Ministry of Transport spent its funding and loans in 2016.

A member of the Egyptian Parliament and leader of the Justice Party, Abdel Moneim Imam, told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the continued “turning of a blind eye to the shortcomings and the recurrence of accidents without genuine accountability leads to the continuation of the crisis”.

articles.title: Putin showed ‘restraint’ by not using nuclear weapons, Kushner says
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has “shown restraint” by not using nuclear weapons in the conflict with Ukraine, White House envoy Jared Kushner has said, while describing the Russian leader as a “grand man of politics.”
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has “shown restraint” by not using nuclear weapons in the conflict with Ukraine, White House envoy Jared Kushner has said, while describing the Russian leader as a “grand man of politics.” In a wide-ranging interview for Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner’s “MD Meets” podcast, Kushner – who is President Donald Trump’s son-in-law – said he was convinced Putin wanted peace. “My assessment is that he does not only want peace; he wants to try and change the relationship with America, and he does want to try and see if there’s maybe a way to start a new beginning.” “So far Putin has showed restraint; he’s agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing, and he’s reassured us that that’s not his intention,” he added. Kushner and his fellow US negotiator Steve Witkoff have met Putin several times, most recently this month at the Kremlin. “He’s definitely a grand man of politics, he’s a historic figure,” Kushner said. “He takes a lot of notes when we’re speaking, and he transmits very specifically. But it’s very clear he has a very deep understanding of the issues.” Kushner rejected suggestions that the US had applied pressure on Ukraine to make concessions to Russia. Ukraine has said that the US Defense Department has delayed shipments of vital air defense missiles and intelligence sharing has been disrupted. As for efforts to reach a settlement that would include issues of territorial control, Kushner said: “This isn’t about fairness or who’s right or wrong.” Kushner said border lines in Europe had changed over time. “I do believe that when people see long-term durability and a pathway to peace, I think they’ll be a little bit more flexible on where do you draw the line.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this month that US negotiators had floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for membership of NATO. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said after meeting Kushner and Witkoff. Ukraine has long resisted the idea of ceding land to Russia, which launched an unprovoked full-scale invasion in 2022. Zelensky said if he received a “comprehensive security package” – which would include a strong Ukrainian army and guarantees from NATO and the European Union – he would put a proposal to the public. Alluding to that possibility, Kushner told Politico, “Without a security guarantee from America, Ukraine will not be safe in the future… President Trump has to determine that a security guarantee is in the interests of America to give.” Zelensky has previously said that Russia would not stop at taking the Donbas – whose two regions comprise nearly 10% of Ukrainian territory – but would plan further attacks. As for negotiations, Kushner said: “I wish there was a fast way to do this… There’s a lot we agree on. We all want long-term peace.” “Once we’re able to define that post-war relationship, I think the issue of territory will become much easier to resolve because right now there’s no way to bridge that last issue.” Without a settlement there was a real risk of escalation, Kushner said. “Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia, and it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively,” Kushner warned. The ultimate goal, Kushner said, was that “if you can end this war in a way where Ukraine is sovereign, secure, prosperous, and free, they could join the EU. They have a post-war economy plan. They have credible security guarantees. They have strong deterrence capabilities. That’s a huge victory for Ukraine and for Europe.”

articles.title: Norse Atlantic suspends all flights as it faces potential collapse
articles.summary: The carrier is looking for urgent funding, but will file for bankruptcy without a financial lifeline.
articles.body:
The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.

The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.

The airline uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.

Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.

One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.

The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.

PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.

In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.

Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."

Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.

Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.

It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.

But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.

Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.

This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.

In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.

In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.

After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".

However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Norse Atlantic had been looking for a buyer since July.

Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.

If Norse Atlantic were to fold, it would be another major setback for the low-cost long-haul model, which has typically proved popular with passengers but difficult to sustain financially, especially on transatlantic routes.

articles.title: Ethan Ives-Griffiths murder: Every day is 'living hell' says dad
articles.summary: Ethan Ives-Griffiths' father says concerns about his son's safety "weren't heard" before his murder.
articles.body:
A father who raised concerns about the grandparents who murdered his two-year-old son says that every day without him has been "living hell".

Ethan Ives-Griffiths died on 16 August 2021 after suffering a "catastrophic" head injury at his grandparents' home in Garden City, Flintshire.

Michael Ives, 49, and Kerry Ives, 47, were jailed for life in 2025. Ethan's mum, Shannon Ives, 29, was jailed for 12 years for causing or allowing his death and child cruelty.

A review into Ethan's death found that his father, Will Griffiths, raised concerns about his safety, but they were not acted on, and opportunities to protect Ethan were missed by multiple agencies .

Griffiths said he believed his son would "still be alive today" if his concerns had been acted upon.

"I wasn't being heard," he said, adding he was "still stuck in 2021" and unable to move past the day Ethan died.

"I haven't felt like I've lived. I've just been existing, waiting for everything to come out slowly."

Griffiths said it "disgusted" him that the police "didn't listen" when he told them he believed Ethan and his other children were not safe around the grandparents.

"They made threats and they've shown in every way, shape and form since day one they are a threat to my children," he said.

Warning: This article contains details of violence and abuse that some may find distressing

When Griffiths and Ethan's mother split in June 2021, police in attendance noted Griffiths was "begging" the social worker not to take Ethan to his grandparents, but there was no record that was shared with the children's service.

Children's services were informed on 7 July that Ethan was living with his grandparents, but there was no record of any checks being made about his welfare and his address was not changed on the IT system, the review found.

The Ives family were well known to health and education services, Flintshire council's children's services, and North Wales Police, because of issues surrounding "significant domestic violence", substance abuse and homelessness.

The review highlighted 36 referrals and concerns raised about Ethan or his immediate family since 2016.

Griffiths described it as "horrible" knowing that "anything could be going on" and he could not do anything about it.

During the seven weeks Ethan lived with them, he became severely malnourished and dehydrated, and had more than 40 injuries on his body when he died.

Allegations were raised against Griffiths for "significant domestic abuse" towards Shannon, as well as "substance misuse".

Speaking to the BBC, Griffiths denied accusations of domestic abuse, neglect and assault.

He admitted smoking cannabis but said he never smoked around his children and did not consider his use "to a point of misuse or abusing".

When asked why the father's concerns were not acted upon, the director of social services, Craig MacLeod, said they were "focusing on domestic violence and emotional harm".

"We weren't fully attuned to the risk presented by the grandparents," he added.

The council apologised to Griffiths and said it would work to strengthen its approach to "engaging with fathers and male carers in our work with families".

"It's absolutely ruined my mental health, my family's mental health, having to deal with this year after year after - the appeals, the sentencing, the trial, all of it," Griffiths said.

"It has been so much. It really has. And it just felt like it's never ending."

Speaking of the review's findings, he said he did not need a piece of paper to tell him "you were right, we were wrong" as he knew what he was reporting "from day one".

"The closure we have now is more for just my own gratification of knowing that I was right about them the whole time."

"There is no closure on Ethan's death or any of that. I don't believe there will ever be closure on that."

He added that he believed Ethan "would still be alive today" if an intervention had been made "at any point".

Griffiths said he hoped the findings of the review would now enable "many, many more children to be saved and protected properly".

"I also believe and hope that men get listened to a lot more," he added.

North Wales Safeguarding Board apologised "unreservedly" after the review's findings, while Flintshire council admitted it had "failed" Ethan and was "deeply sorry".

Ch Supt Sian Beck, of North Wales Police, said she recognised "the strength and courage of Ethan's father" throughout the investigation.

"We recognise there were areas where North Wales Police could have improved its response, and we apologise to Ethan's father, and his family, for this," she said.

She said the force had "co-operated fully with the review" and was "thankful... for their thorough investigation", adding it would now "work closely with our partners to ensure that the learning leads to meaningful improvements".

Rocio Cifuentes, the children's commissioner for Wales, said it was a "really heartbreaking and harrowing" case.

She added there were "consistent themes" of issues around information-sharing and "organisations not effectively letting others know when there are concerns".

"I think that leads us to question of who is really having that oversight and who is making sure that these consistent themes are actually being acted on in a timely way, and that's the gap that I think we still have," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast .
